subject: POLLAK (1964)
object: POLLAK (1964) studied antinuclear antibodies in family members of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus.

subject: LEONHARDT (1964)
object: LEONHARDT (1964) reported family studies in systemic lupus erythematosus.

subject: Siegel et al. (1965)
object: Siegel et al. (1965) carried out a comparative family study of rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus.

subject: Lappat and Cawein (1968)
object: Lappat and Cawein (1968) carried out a family study of procainamide-induced systemic lupus erythematosus. They asked whether a pharmacogenetic polymorphism might underlie susceptibility.

subject: Siegel et al. (1970)
object: Siegel et al. (1970) reported comparative epidemiologic data on systemic lupus erythematosus for New York City and Jefferson County, Alabama, covering 1956 to 1965.

subject: Tuffanelli (1971)
object: Tuffanelli (1971) described lupus erythematosus panniculitis (lupus erythematosus profundus), a form of lupus erythematosus that involves the subcutaneous fat.

subject: Larsen (1972)
object: Larsen (1972) reported family studies in systemic lupus erythematosus based on a group of probands from central eastern Norway.

subject: Reed et al. (1972)
object: Reed et al. (1972) described a hereditary inflammatory vasculitis with persistent nodules. They regarded it as a new, genetically determined entity probably related to lupus erythematosus.

subject: Schaller (1972)
object: Schaller (1972) described an illness resembling lupus erythematosus in mothers of boys with chronic granulomatous disease.

subject: Larsen and Godal (1972)
object: Larsen and Godal (1972) studied thyroid diseases and thyroid antibodies in families of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus, as part of a series of family studies in SLE.

subject: First (1973)
object: First (1973) reported familial occurrence of systemic lupus erythematosus.

subject: Fessel (1974)
object: Fessel (1974) studied the incidence, prevalence, outcome, and first symptoms of systemic lupus erythematosus in the community and found a high prevalence in black women.

subject: Kohler et al. (1974)
object: Kohler et al. (1974) reported identical twin boys who had both hereditary angioedema and 'familial' lupus erythematosus.

subject: DeHoratius et al. (1975)
object: DeHoratius et al. (1975) found anti-RNA antibodies in 82% of 28 SLE probands, 16% of 124 of their family members, and 5% of 76 control family members. Among SLE family members, the antibodies were found only in the 94 close household contacts of the probands, 21% of whom had them. Anti-native DNA antibodies were present in 68% of probands and 6% of close household contacts, compared with 1% in control families; the difference between household contacts and controls was not significant.

subject: DeHoratius et al. (1975)
object: DeHoratius et al. (1975) found lymphocytotoxic antibodies in 57% of SLE family members overall and in 68% of close household contacts. In probands, these antibodies correlated with anti-single-stranded RNA (poly A) and anti-nDNA antibodies; in household contacts, they correlated with anti-double-stranded RNA (poly A-poly U) antibodies. Anti-RNA antibodies occurred in consanguineous household contacts but not in nonconsanguineous ones. The authors concluded that this supported the hypothesis that both an environmental agent, possibly a virus, and the genetic response are important in the pathogenesis of SLE.

subject: Block et al. (1975)
object: Block et al. (1975) studied 12 twin pairs in which one or both twins had SLE (7 definitely monozygotic, 3 definitely dizygotic) and compared them with 17 previously described twin pairs (12 definitely monozygotic). Four of 7 (57%) definitely monozygotic pairs were clinically concordant for SLE by ARA preliminary criteria, and concordance for antinuclear factor and hypergammaglobulinemia was 71% and 87%, respectively, closely agreeing with the 12 previously described monozygotic sets.

subject: Block et al. (1975)
object: Block et al. (1975) found that all 3 dizygotic twin sets in their series were discordant for clinical SLE, although one clinically well twin had marked serologic abnormalities. Comparison with data from other first-degree relatives suggested to the authors a strong genetic component in the pathogenesis of SLE, with nongenetic and environmental factors also contributing to disease expression.

subject: Yocum et al. (1975)
object: Yocum et al. (1975) studied a pair of monozygotic twins discordant for SLE. Both twins had biologically false-positive serologic tests for syphilis at an early age, but only one developed SLE. The twins did not differ in their immune responses to tetanus toxoid, keyhole limpet hemocyanin, or DNCB, in delayed sensitivity, or in antibody titers to viruses.

subject: Yocum et al. (1975)
object: Yocum et al. (1975) noted that the clinically unaffected twin of a monozygotic pair discordant for SLE had been castrated at an early age. They suggested that ovarian hormones may play an important role in the development of SLE.

subject: Arnett and Shulman (1976)
object: Arnett and Shulman (1976) studied 8 families with familial SLE. Combining these with 1 deceased pair and 31 families from the literature gave 8 pairs of identical twins, 1 pair of non-identical twins, 16 sibling combinations and 15 parent-offspring combinations. Of these, 53 cases in 25 families had enough documentation for detailed analysis. The authors compared 23 clinical and laboratory features between affected relatives and against matched non-related SLE controls. They found impressive concordance for disease expression between identical twins and between parents and offspring, but not between siblings or controls. They concluded that this supported genetic influences on how SLE is expressed.

subject: Arnett and Shulman (1976)
object: Arnett and Shulman (1976) found 4 father-offspring pairs among families with familial SLE. They stated that this made it less likely that SLE is transmitted during the perinatal period.

subject: Arnett and Shulman (1976)
object: Arnett and Shulman (1976) found that SLE began in each member of an identical twin pair within an average of 2 years of each other. Between siblings, the average difference in age at onset was 9 years, but the average difference in actual calendar date of onset was only 3 years. For parents and offspring, the corresponding figures were 20 and 8 years. The authors suggested that environmental influences play a role in starting SLE, especially in siblings.

subject: Arnett and Shulman (1976)
object: Arnett and Shulman (1976) found no real differences in the frequencies of clinical and laboratory features between familial and non-familial SLE. They concluded that familial SLE is probably not a different disease entity from non-familial SLE.

subject: Arnett and Shulman (1976)
object: Arnett and Shulman (1976) studied 27 unaffected first-degree relatives in their 8 families. Two sisters had thyroid disease, persistent leukopenia and a raised sedimentation rate. Their mother had SLE and Hashimoto thyroiditis, and their sibling had SLE. The other 25 relatives were normal clinically, hematologically, biochemically and serologically.

subject: Beaucher et al. (1977)
object: Beaucher et al. (1977) reported familial lupus erythematosus together with antibodies to DNA in household dogs.

subject: Brustein et al. (1977)
object: Brustein et al. (1977) reported familial lupus erythematosus. A woman had discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE), and her child developed DLE lesions at 2 months of age. The original lesions persisted and new lesions kept appearing up to the time of the report, when the child was 28 months old. In a second child, then 11 months old, a probable lupus erythematosus rash developed at 1 week of age.

subject: Horn et al. (1978)
object: Horn et al. (1978) described a brother and sister with mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) and studied 18 additional family members spanning 3 generations; 8 relatives had symptoms or signs of MCTD without complete expression of the disease. Antibodies to ribonucleoprotein and high-titer antinuclear antibodies were found only in the affected sibs, while rheumatoid factor was positive in 9 of 17 relatives, with titers ranging from 1:160 to 1:2560.

subject: Horn et al. (1978)
object: Horn et al. (1978) found that the brother and sister with MCTD had an identical HLA genotype (11,12/2,12), which was also inherited by 3 of their sibs who had impressive rheumatic complaints; the authors emphasized the association between inflammatory connective tissue disease and a specific HLA type within a single kindred.

subject: Knight and Adams (1978)
object: Knight and Adams (1978) studied the incidence of early severe lupus nephritis, identified by antemortem determination of renal function, in 230 (NZB x NZW) x NZW backcross mice and 150 (NZB x NZW) x NZB backcross mice. The data indicated that the NZB strain contributes only 1 gene and the NZW strain contributes 2 genes, or clusters of closely linked genes, to the renal disorder of the F1 hybrid; neither parental inbred strain shows the disorder. All 3 genes were concluded to be dominant or codominant, as their effect is expressed in the heterozygous state.

subject: Knight and Adams (1978)
object: In (NZB x NZW) backcross mice, Knight and Adams (1978) found that 1 of the 2 NZW-derived genes contributing to lupus nephritis was linked to the H-2 (major histocompatibility) complex.

subject: Miller and Schwartz (1979)
object: Miller and Schwartz (1979) used an in vitro suppressor-cell assay to evaluate central immunoregulation in 15 patients with SLE, 50 of their clinically healthy family members, and 41 normal persons. Impaired suppressor-cell function was found in 11 of the 15 patients, with no correlation between disease activity and test results.

subject: Miller and Schwartz (1979)
object: Miller and Schwartz (1979) found abnormal suppressor-cell activity in 13 clinically healthy first-degree relatives of SLE patients, 12 of whom were women, with no correlation between assay results and lymphocytotoxic antibodies in relatives. They concluded that impaired suppressor-cell function cannot by itself explain SLE pathogenesis, that certain suppressor-cell abnormalities are genetic markers, and proposed that development of SLE requires participation of at least two functionally distinct classes of genes.

subject: Serdula and Rhoads (1979)
object: Serdula and Rhoads (1979) surveyed SLE patients in civilian general hospitals on Oahu, Hawaii, for 1970-1975 and ascertained 168 cases, 107 considered definite. Age-adjusted prevalence rates per 100,000 for definite cases at the end of 1975 were 5.8 in whites, 24.1 in Chinese, 19.9 in Filipinos, 20.4 in part-Hawaiians, and 18.2 in Japanese. Females made up about 90% of definite cases overall, with a heavy female preponderance in each ethnic group.

subject: Serdula and Rhoads (1979)
object: Serdula and Rhoads (1979) reviewed vital statistics and found age-adjusted SLE mortality rates per million of 3.04 for US whites, 8.82 for US nonwhites, 1.89 for Hawaii whites, and 14.46 for Hawaii nonwhites. They stated that the cause of the very high SLE prevalence and mortality in the Oriental and Polynesian people of Hawaii was not clear.

subject: Batchelor et al. (1980)
object: Batchelor et al. (1980) studied 26 patients with SLE induced by the antihypertensive drug hydralazine; 25 of the 26 were slow acetylators. HLA-DR4 frequency was 73% in hydralazine-induced SLE, significantly higher than in 113 healthy controls (33%), 16 slow-acetylator hypertensive patients treated with hydralazine for more than a year without developing SLE (25%), and 20 patients with idiopathic SLE (25%).

subject: Batchelor et al. (1980)
object: Batchelor et al. (1980) found a 4:1 ratio of women to men among patients with hydralazine-induced SLE. When all slow acetylators treated with hydralazine were analysed together, every woman with DR4 developed SLE, and the only men who did were those with DR2 who were receiving 200 mg hydralazine per day.

subject: Batchelor et al. (1980)
object: Batchelor et al. (1980) found that the distribution of HLA-DR antigens in hydralazine-induced SLE differed significantly from that in idiopathic SLE. They concluded that this supports the view that the two syndromes are separate entities.

subject: Reidenberg et al. (1980)
object: Reidenberg et al. (1980) used dapsone or isoniazid to determine acetylator phenotype in 50 patients with idiopathic SLE, 21 from New York City and 29 from Israel. Thirty were slow acetylators, 17 were rapid acetylators, and 3 were indeterminate. When these cases were combined with published studies, the worldwide distribution in idiopathic SLE was 150 slow to 77 rapid acetylators, compared with an expected 122:105 (P less than 0.001).

subject: Exner et al. (1980)
object: Exner et al. (1980) found a lupus anticoagulant in the plasma of 2 pairs of sibs using the kaolin clotting time mixing test. They also presented strong evidence for this inhibitor in a third sib pair.

subject: Exner et al. (1980)
object: Exner et al. (1980) concluded that the lupus anticoagulant might often be an acquired coagulation defect that requires a genetic predisposition.

subject: Weinberg et al. (1980)
object: Weinberg et al. (1980) studied a large pedigree ascertained through one individual who had elliptocytosis, multiple lipomatosis, and a biological false-positive serologic test for syphilis (BFPSTS). They tested 180 relatives. Two female members of the pedigree who had BFPSTS developed systemic lupus erythematosus, which the authors noted agreed with the previously described association. The analysis did not lead to any conclusion about a causal relationship between the two traits.

subject: Weinberg et al. (1980)
object: In the pedigree studied by Weinberg et al. (1980), BFPSTS appeared to be inherited as a dominant trait, but the likelihood analysis was inconclusive. The same analysis confirmed that elliptocytosis and lipomatosis were each inherited independently as dominant traits.

subject: Weinberg et al. (1980)
object: Weinberg et al. (1980) typed 74 relatives for 7 blood group antigens and 58 relatives for 4 electrophoretic enzyme markers. They found no linkage between any of the disease genes, including the one for BFPSTS, and any of the marker genes.

subject: Tan et al. (1982)
object: Tan et al. (1982) revised the 1971 preliminary criteria for the classification of SLE to incorporate new immunologic knowledge, adding fluorescence antinuclear antibody and antibody to native DNA and Sm antigen. They combined some criteria for the same organ system into single criteria. They dropped Raynaud phenomenon and alopecia because of low sensitivity and specificity. When tested with SLE and control patient data from 18 participating clinics, the revised criteria were 96% sensitive and 96% specific, which was better than the 1971 criteria.

subject: Solomon et al. (1983)
object: Solomon et al. (1983) purified anti-native DNA antibodies from the serum of a patient with active SLE and used them to raise mouse monoclonal anti-idiotypic antibodies. One of these, 3I (IgG2a kappa), recognized an idiotypic determinant outside the antigen-binding site. In a solid-phase radioimmunoassay, 3I reacted with 8 of 9 sera that contained anti-native DNA activity. The authors suggested that anti-native DNA antibodies from unrelated SLE patients share a common idiotype.

subject: Fielder et al. (1983)
object: Fielder et al. (1983) studied the families of 29 patients with SLE and 42 normal subjects to determine inheritance of HLA-A, B, C, and DR antigens and the complement polymorphisms C2, C4A, C4B, and Bf. Null (silent) alleles for C4A, C4B, or C2 were found in 24 of 29 (83%) patients compared with 18 of 42 (43%) normal controls.

subject: Fielder et al. (1983)
object: Fielder et al. (1983) found HLA-DR3 in 20 of 29 (69%) SLE patients versus 7 of 39 (18%) normal controls, with strong linkage disequilibrium between DR3 and the null alleles of C4A and C4B, so that the relative contributions of DR3 and C4 null alleles as risk factors could not be distinguished.

subject: Fielder et al. (1983)
object: Fielder et al. (1983) suggested that, given the known association of SLE with inherited and acquired complement deficiencies, the presence of null alleles for C4A, C4B, and C2 in most patients is relevant to their genetic susceptibility to SLE.

subject: Reveille et al. (1983)
object: Reveille et al. (1983) studied 8 families containing 2 or more members with SLE (22 patients) and 40 relatives. Among the 40 non-SLE relatives, 7 (18%) had other immune diseases (thyroid disease in 2, rheumatoid arthritis in 2, ITP in 2, Henoch-Schonlein purpura in 1), compared with 4 of the 22 SLE patients (3 with thyroid disease and 1 with PSS). Eleven non-SLE relatives (28%) had ANA, high-titer in 5, and 11 had antibodies to ssDNA; only SLE patients had anti-dsDNA, Ro(SSA), Sm, or nRNP antibodies.

subject: Reveille et al. (1983)
object: In these families, Reveille et al. (1983) found heterozygous C2 deficiency in only 1 of 7 kindreds studied, segregating with an A25, B18, DR7 haplotype, and inherited by only 1 of 3 family members with SLE. HLA-DR2 and DR3 each occurred in 36% of SLE patients, not significantly different from non-SLE relatives or controls, and sib-pair analysis of 14 sets showed only random HLA distribution with SLE. The authors concluded that genetic factors other than HLA and complement deficiencies and/or environmental factors are necessary for expression of SLE.

subject: Lahita et al. (1983)
object: Lahita et al. (1983) described several families in which systemic lupus erythematosus occurred mainly in males, affecting mostly the sons and the fathers. In some families, female members had other autoimmune diseases, such as idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, or symptoms suggestive of a lupus diathesis. The authors noted that the disease in these patients was somewhat similar to the disease in BXSB mice.

subject: Lahita et al. (1983)
object: Lahita et al. (1983) suggested that in these families with mainly male systemic lupus erythematosus, the sons inherited the disease from their fathers.

subject: Steinberg et al. (1984)
object: Steinberg et al. (1984) described systemic lupus erythematosus as a multisystem, antibody-mediated autoimmune disorder occurring spontaneously in humans and mice, in which genetic factors play an important predisposing role: some genes may produce a generalized immune abnormality, whereas others may lead to specific autoantibodies, and environmental triggers increase autoantibody production and augment expression of illness.

subject: Steinberg et al. (1984)
object: Steinberg et al. (1984) proposed that bacterial and viral illnesses activate macrophages and T cells that stimulate B cells; in the absence of normal control mechanisms the stimulation is not suppressed, excessive stem cell proliferation leads to abnormal B-cell proliferation, and the signal for proliferating B cells to differentiate into antibody-forming cells triggers disease.

subject: Steinberg et al. (1984)
object: Steinberg et al. (1984) reported that most autoantibody-producing B cells can be eliminated from lupus-prone mice by the presence of the xid gene, and that administration of an arachidonic acid analog was an effective treatment for murine lupus.

subject: Diamond and Scharff (1984)
object: Diamond and Scharff (1984) studied U4, a somatic mutant of the S107 mouse myeloma line, which makes an antiphosphocholine antibody of the T15 idiotype. U4 produced an immunoglobulin with a single substitution of alanine for glutamic acid at residue 35 of the T15 heavy chain. This change abolished phosphocholine binding, but the antibody gained reactivity with phosphorylated macromolecules including double-stranded DNA, protamine, and cardiolipin. The authors concluded that a single amino acid change can transform an antibacterial antibody into one that resembles the autoantibodies seen in autoimmune disease in mice and humans.

subject: Stohl et al. (1985)
object: Stohl et al. (1985) described 3 black Jamaican patients with SLE whose T helper/inducer cells lacked the T4 epitope (T4 epitope-deficient phenotype). All 3 patients had lymphadenopathy. The asymptomatic, otherwise healthy T4 epitope-deficient brother of one patient also had lymphadenopathy in the same distribution as his sister with SLE.

subject: Stohl et al. (1985)
object: Family studies by Stohl et al. (1985) indicated autosomal codominant inheritance of the T4 epitope phenotype, not linked to the HLA locus.

subject: Stohl et al. (1985)
object: Stohl et al. (1985) found that peripheral blood mononuclear cells from T4 epitope-deficient family members showed impaired B-cell differentiation after pokeweed mitogen stimulation compared with cells from T4 epitope-intermediate relatives. Helper/suppressor T-cell ratios, autoantibodies, mitogen proliferation, and mixed lymphocyte reactions did not correlate with T4 epitope phenotype. The authors suggested that SLE with the T4 epitope-deficient phenotype may be a distinct subset of SLE.

subject: Halpern et al. (1985)
object: Halpern et al. (1985) used radioimmunoassay to test sera from 27 members of 3 kindreds with familial SLE for a cross-reactive idiotype found on anti-DNA antibodies, detected with the antiidiotype 3I. High-titered reactivity was present in 6 of 8 SLE patients and 15 of 19 family members. The authors concluded that expression of this idiotype was significantly increased in relatives of SLE patients and usually occurred without anti-DNA activity.

subject: Halpern et al. (1985)
object: In the familial SLE kindreds studied by Halpern et al. (1985), Millipore filter analysis found anti-DNA antibodies in 4 of 8 SLE patients and in 2 of 19 family members without SLE. Under conditions that dissociate immune complexes, anti-DNA antibodies were also found in 2 more patients and 2 more family members. On isoelectric focusing, cationic 3I-reactive bands (pH 7-8.5) correlated with the presence of anti-DNA antibodies, which the authors took to indicate that immunoglobulin charge may help determine specificity for DNA.

subject: Theofilopoulos and Dixon (1985)
object: Theofilopoulos and Dixon (1985) reviewed murine models of systemic lupus erythematosus.

subject: Green et al. (1986)
object: Green et al. (1986) used the empirical logistic method to analyze data, including the relevant genotypes, on the reported associations of SLE with HLA-DR3 and with null (QO) alleles at the C4A and C4B loci. The analysis suggested that the association with C4 null alleles was primary and that the DR3 association was likely secondary to it, which might help locate the HLA-linked disease susceptibility gene.

subject: Baer et al. (1986)
object: Baer et al. (1986) found that the slow acetylator phenotype was about as common in 64 patients with idiopathic SLE (38%) as in 60 healthy volunteers (50%) and 52 non-SLE medical service patients (44%). Slow acetylators were not more frequent in SLE subgroups defined by demographic features or by specific disease manifestations. The authors concluded that their results, like most previously published results, gave no evidence for an association between acetylator phenotype and idiopathic SLE.

subject: Fronek et al. (1986)
object: Fronek et al. (1986) examined genomic DNA restriction fragment length polymorphisms (RFLPs) of the T cell receptor beta chain gene in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus, their relatives, and normal controls, and found a similar RFLP distribution in all groups. They suggested that the TCR beta chain genes are not coinherited with genes responsible for SLE.

subject: Mackie et al. (1987)
object: Mackie et al. (1987) studied 3 families in which more than one member had SLE or lupus-like disease. Of the 19 people studied, 11 had SLE or lupus-like disease. In 8 of these 11, the kaolin partial thromboplastin time (KPTT) was prolonged and there was other evidence of lupus anticoagulant. Only 5 of the 11 had high anticardiolipin antibody titers.

subject: Mackie et al. (1987)
object: Mackie et al. (1987) found a prolonged KPTT that did not correct on mixing in 4 healthy spouses of affected women and in 3 asymptomatic sibs. None of these 7 people had a history of bleeding or thrombosis, and their clotting factor levels were normal. The authors concluded that these findings would support the idea that transmissible agents or other environmental factors are involved in lupus-like disorders.

subject: Mackie et al. (1987)
object: Mackie et al. (1987) found that anticardiolipin levels were raised in subjects with lupus anticoagulant. However, the length of the KPTT did not correlate closely with the anticardiolipin titer.

subject: Wong et al. (1988)
object: Wong et al. (1988) used Southern blot analysis of restriction fragment length polymorphisms (RFLPs) to study the T cell receptor (TcR) alpha, beta and gamma chain genes in 5 families with multiple members affected by SLE, 14 unrelated SLE patients and 14 normal controls. Polymorphic patterns were found with probes for all 3 TcR chains. However, the distribution of RFLP patterns did not differ significantly among patients, relatives and controls, and none of the 3 TcR genes cosegregated with the disease in families with at least 2 affected members. The authors concluded that the TcR alpha, beta and gamma chain genes are not likely to be linked to genes related to SLE.

subject: Levcovitz et al. (1988)
object: Levcovitz et al. (1988) found that every SLE patient they studied had two classes of newly synthesized DNA in sucrose density gradients of PHA-stimulated lymphocytes. One was a large-molecular-weight fraction that comigrated with control DNA. The other was an excess low-molecular-weight DNA (LMW-DNA) fraction not seen in control lymphocytes. The excess LMW-DNA did not depend on disease activity or drug therapy.

subject: Levcovitz et al. (1988)
object: Levcovitz et al. (1988) studied a four-generation family in which two first cousins had SLE. Excess lymphocyte LMW-DNA was present in both cousins, in their parents (who were siblings), in a common grandparent, in 4 of 9 siblings of one patient, and in 5 of 7 at-risk children. Every unaffected adult relative with the marker had positive antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) except the grandmother. None of the 5 children with excess LMW-DNA had positive ANAs.

subject: Levcovitz et al. (1988)
object: In the family studied by Levcovitz et al. (1988), excess LMW-DNA occurred in both males and females and was passed from male to male. The authors concluded that excess LMW-DNA in stimulated lymphocytes was inherited as an autosomal dominant trait in this family.

subject: Levcovitz et al. (1988)
object: Levcovitz et al. (1988) concluded that, in children of adults with excess LMW-DNA, the excess LMW-DNA appears before ANAs. They suggested it may be a predisposing factor in the development of the immunologic responses of SLE.

subject: Sakane et al. (1989)
object: Sakane et al. (1989) studied 34 clinically healthy family members of 6 SLE probands using a phytohemagglutinin-induced IL-2 activity assay (T-cell function) and a spontaneous plaque-forming cell assay (B-cell function). Impaired IL-2 activity was found in 15 of 29 blood relatives but in none of 5 nonconsanguineous household members, and was unrelated to household status, leading the authors to conclude that impaired IL-2 activity strongly correlates with a genetic relationship.

subject: Sakane et al. (1989)
object: Sakane et al. (1989) found abnormal spontaneous B-cell immunoglobulin secretion (plaque-forming cell assay) in 22 of 29 blood relatives of SLE probands, more commonly in consanguineous household relatives, but also in 4 of 5 nonconsanguineous household members. They concluded that although the evidence favored a genetic basis for the B-cell abnormalities, environmental effects may also contribute to their familial occurrence.

subject: Sturfelt et al. (1990)
object: Sturfelt et al. (1990) found homozygous C4A deficiency in 16% (13 of 80) of SLE patients. The patients were all diagnosed cases ascertained from a defined population in southern Sweden, which the authors said minimized patient selection bias.

subject: Sturfelt et al. (1990)
object: Sturfelt et al. (1990) found that photosensitivity was more common in SLE patients with C4A deficiency than in other SLE patients (p less than 0.05). Other clinical features were similar between the groups, and the authors found no differences in anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-RNP, anti-SSA, anti-SSB, rheumatoid factor or anticardiolipin antibodies. They noted that the increased photosensitivity partly resembled findings in patients with complete deficiencies of classical pathway components.

subject: Sturfelt et al. (1990)
object: Sturfelt et al. (1990) found that in SLE patients expressing both C4A and C4B isotypes, plasma C4B/C4A quotients stayed fairly stable regardless of disease activity. The authors said this argued against preferential breakdown of either isotype during complement activation in SLE.

subject: Sibley et al. (1993)
object: Sibley et al. (1993) described a family in which 3 members each developed systemic lupus erythematosus complicated by ischemic vasculopathy (digital ischemia). The calendar years and patient ages of disease onset and the clinical courses were remarkably similar in all 3 patients, although their genotypes were not.

subject: Sibley et al. (1993)
object: Sibley et al. (1993) discussed the potential contributions of heredity and environment to the concordance of disease expression (similar onset in calendar time and age) in a family with 3 members affected by SLE.

subject: Morel et al. (1994)
object: Morel et al. (1994) studied susceptibility to glomerulonephritis and anti-dsDNA autoantibody production in a newly developed lupus-susceptible inbred mouse strain, NZM/Aeg2410. Using interval mapping in a backcross with C57BL/6, they found 3 chromosomal intervals on mouse chromosomes 1, 4, and 7 that carried strong recessive glomerulonephritis susceptibility alleles. Heterozygosity at H-2 also correlated strongly with susceptibility to glomerulonephritis.

subject: Morel et al. (1994)
object: Morel et al. (1994) used logistic regression analysis in the NZM/Aeg2410 mouse model. It indicated that each susceptibility allele independently accounted for part of the susceptibility to glomerulonephritis, and that susceptibility was inherited as a threshold genetic liability.

subject: Schur (1995)
object: Schur (1995) reviewed the genetics of systemic lupus erythematosus.

subject: Kotzin (1996)
object: Kotzin (1996) reviewed systemic lupus erythematosus.

subject: Wu et al. (1996)
object: Wu et al. (1996) used SSCP analysis to screen the extracellular domain of FASL in DNA from 75 patients with SLE. They found a heterozygous change in 1 patient, who had lymphadenopathy. Cloning and sequencing showed an 84-bp deletion within exon 4 of the FASL gene, predicted to cause an in-frame deletion of 28 amino acids. The authors suggested that FASL mutations are an uncommon cause of SLE.

subject: FASLG 84-bp deletion within exon 4 of the fasL gene, resulting in a predicted 28 amino acid in-frame deletion
object: FASLG

subject: Wu et al. (1996)
object: Wu et al. (1996) found that PBMCs from the SLE patient with the heterozygous 84-bp FASL deletion had reduced FasL activity and reduced activation-induced cell death, and their T cells proliferated more after activation. The authors described this as the first report of defective FasL-mediated apoptosis linked to a mutation in the human FASL gene in a patient with SLE.

subject: FASLG 84-bp deletion within exon 4 of the fasL gene
object: FASLG

subject: Vyse et al. (1996)
object: Vyse et al. (1996) performed a genetic analysis of (NZB x NZW)F1 x NZW backcross mice, a model of human SLE with severe immune complex-mediated nephritis. One set of loci coordinately regulated serum levels of IgG antibodies to double-stranded DNA, single-stranded DNA, total histones, and chromatin. These loci overlapped with loci linked to production of autoantibodies to the viral glycoprotein gp70.

subject: Vyse et al. (1996)
object: In (NZB x NZW)F1 x NZW backcross mice, Vyse et al. (1996) found that loci linked with anti-gp70 antibodies showed stronger linkage with renal disease than loci linked with antinuclear antibodies. They suggested that autoantibodies to gp70 are the major pathogenic antibodies in this model of lupus nephritis. A distal chromosome 4 locus, Nba1, was linked with nephritis but with none of the autoantibodies measured. The authors suggested that Nba1 contributes to renal disease at a checkpoint distal to autoantibody production.

subject: García et al. (1996)
object: García et al. (1996) looked at autoantibody profiles in 222 African-American patients with SLE: 94 had lupus nephritis and 128 did not. Anti-dsDNA was the only antibody that differed significantly between the 2 groups (P less than 0.05). Positive anti-Ro/SS-A, anti-Sm, and anti-nRNP without anti-La/SS-B was seen in 14 (14.9%) patients with nephritis and 15 (11.7%) without it (P greater than 0.6). The authors concluded that African-American SLE patients with lupus nephritis do not have a specific or distinctive autoantibody profile, but that their data confirmed the value of anti-dsDNA in these patients.

subject: Sanghera et al. (1997)
object: Sanghera et al. (1997) identified a common missense mutation at codon 316 (TGG-to-TCG) in the fifth domain of apolipoprotein H (APOH; beta-2-glycoprotein I), resulting in a trp316-to-ser substitution. The authors stated that it disrupted a highly conserved sequence of 4 hydrophobic amino acids at positions 313 to 316, which is a potential site of protein-lipid hydrophobic interaction. ApoH from the 2 Ser316 homozygotes did not bind negatively charged phosphatidylserine, whereas heterozygotes bound it normally.

subject: APOH p.W316S
object: APOH

subject: Sanghera et al. (1997)
object: Sanghera et al. (1997) identified a common missense mutation at codon 306 (TGC-to-GGC) in the fifth domain of APOH, resulting in a cys306-to-gly substitution. They reported that it disrupted the disulfide bond between cys281 and cys306 and altered the normal configuration of the fifth domain. ApoH from all 7 compound heterozygotes for Ser316 and Gly306 did not bind phosphatidylserine, whereas heterozygotes at either site bound it normally.

subject: APOH p.C306G
object: APOH

subject: Sanghera et al. (1997)
object: Sanghera et al. (1997) concluded that the lipid-binding region of APOH lies in its fifth domain. They suggested that about 2 million Caucasians in the United States who are compound heterozygous for the Ser316 and Gly306 mutations may be unable to produce apoH-dependent antiphospholipid autoantibodies.

subject: Elçioglu and Hall (1998)
object: Elçioglu and Hall (1998) described 2 sibs with chondrodysplasia punctata whose mother had systemic lupus erythematosus, described their radiologic features, and compared them with other forms of chondrodysplasia punctata. They highlighted a possible association between maternal SLE and chondrodysplasia punctata in offspring, raising the question of phenocopy versus coincidence.

subject: Austin-Ward et al. (1998)
object: Austin-Ward et al. (1998) reported a newborn infant whose mother had systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed before pregnancy. The child had clinical manifestations of neonatal lupus as well as chondrodysplasia punctata and other findings resembling the congenital anomalies associated with oral anticoagulant use, although there was no history of exposure.

subject: Austin-Ward et al. (1998)
object: Austin-Ward et al. (1998) speculated that the combined action of the different maternal autoantibodies may produce the whole spectrum of manifestations in their infant with neonatal lupus and chondrodysplasia punctata.

subject: Toriello (1998)
object: Toriello (1998) reported chondrodysplasia punctata in association with maternal systemic lupus erythematosus.

subject: Gaffney et al. (1998)
object: Gaffney et al. (1998) performed a genome-wide microsatellite marker screen in 105 SLE sib-pair families. Using multipoint nonparametric methods, the strongest evidence for linkage was found near the HLA locus on 6p11-p21 (D6S257, lod = 3.90, P = 0.000011), with additional linkage at 16q13 (D16S415, lod = 3.64, P = 0.000022), 14q21-q23 (D14S276, lod = 2.81, P = 0.00016), and 20p12 (D20S186, lod = 2.62, P = 0.00025).

subject: Gaffney et al. (1998)
object: Gaffney et al. (1998) identified 9 further regions with lod scores of 1.00 or greater in their SLE sib-pair genome scan: 1p36, 1p13, 1q42, 2p15, 2q21-q33, 3cent-q11, 4q28, 11p15, and 15q26.

subject: Gaffney et al. (1998)
object: Gaffney et al. (1998) concluded that their data supported the hypothesis that multiple genes, including one in the HLA region, influence susceptibility to human SLE.

subject: Shai et al. (1999)
object: Shai et al. (1999) performed a genome-wide screen with 350 polymorphic markers (average spacing 12 cM) in 188 lupus patients from 80 families with 2 or more affected relatives. Nonparametric multipoint linkage analysis suggested predisposing loci on chromosomes 1 and 18, but no single locus showed overwhelming evidence for linkage, suggesting that there are no 'major' susceptibility genes and that the genetic etiology more likely results from several genes of moderate effect.

subject: Shai et al. (1999)
object: Shai et al. (1999) found that support for an SLE susceptibility gene in the 1q44 and 1p36 regions was clearly found only in Mexican American families and not in families of Caucasian ethnicity, suggesting that each ethnic group should be considered separately.

subject: Kelly et al. (1999)
object: Kelly et al. (1999) reported a male infant whose neonatal radiographs showed stippled epiphyses (chondrodysplasia punctata). He then developed a typical lupus erythematosus rash, and his skin findings led to a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus in his mother. Over 3 years of follow-up, the child had strikingly short stature, midface hypoplasia, anomalous digital development, slow resolution of the stippled epiphyses, and near normal cognitive development. The authors reviewed the literature supporting maternal lupus as one cause of chondrodysplasia punctata.

subject: Mohan et al. (1999)
object: Mohan et al. (1999) studied the lupus nephritis susceptibility loci Sle1 and Sle3 from the NZM2410 mouse strain. Mice congenic for Sle1 alone (B6.NZMc1) lost tolerance to chromatin but did not develop pathogenic autoantibodies or disease. Mice congenic for Sle3 alone (B6.NZMc7) showed low-grade polyclonal B- and T-cell activation, elevated CD4/CD8 ratios, and mildly penetrant glomerulonephritis. In contrast, bicongenic B6.NZMc1|c7 mice carrying both loci had splenomegaly, expanded populations of activated B cells and CD4+ T cells, and a robust, varied IgG autoantibody response. The targets included chromatin components such as double-stranded DNA, intact glomeruli, and basement membrane matrix antigens. The bicongenic mice, especially the females, had highly penetrant glomerulonephritis.

subject: Mohan et al. (1999)
object: Mohan et al. (1999) concluded that their findings strongly supported a two-step epistatic model for how pathogenic, kidney-targeting (nephrophilic) autoantibodies form in lupus. In this model, loci such as Sle1 break tolerance to chromatin, while full pathogenic maturation of the autoantibody response appears to require input from other loci, such as Sle3, and from sex-related factors.

subject: Lessard et al. (1999)
object: Lessard et al. (1999) studied 19 healthy individuals (13 CYP2D6 extensive metabolizers and 6 poor metabolizers) given a single 500-mg oral dose of procainamide, alone and with the CYP2D6 inhibitor quinidine. Urinary nitroprocainamide was measurable in 7 of 13 extensive metabolizers but in none of the poor metabolizers, and was undetectable in everyone during quinidine coadministration. The authors suggested that CYP2D6 is involved in the in vivo N-oxidation of procainamide, forming a metabolite potentially involved in procainamide-induced lupus. They noted that further studies were needed to show whether low CYP2D6 activity, whether genetic or caused by drugs, could prevent the drug-induced lupus syndrome.

subject: Linker-Israeli et al. (1999)
object: Linker-Israeli et al. (1999) genotyped the AT-rich minisatellite in the 3-prime flanking region and the 5-prime promoter-enhancer of the IL6 gene in 146 SLE patients and 139 controls. The 3-prime minisatellite allele distribution differed significantly between SLE patients and controls in both Caucasians (P = 0.001) and African Americans (P = 0.006); short alleles (792 bp or less) were seen exclusively in SLE patients, whereas the 828-bp allele was overrepresented in controls. There was no preferential association of SLE with G/C alleles in the 5-prime region.

subject: IL6 3' AT-rich minisatellite short alleles (< or = 792 bp)
object: IL6

subject: Linker-Israeli et al. (1999)
object: Linker-Israeli et al. (1999) found that B lymphoblastoid cells from patients with 1 or 2 SLE-associated IL6 3-prime minisatellite alleles secreted 3- to 4-fold higher IL-6 levels than cells without these alleles, individuals with SLE-associated alleles had about 4-fold higher percentages of IL-6-positive monocytes, and IL-6 mRNA stability was significantly enhanced in lupus patients carrying SLE-associated alleles, suggesting biologic significance of these alleles.

subject: Lindqvist et al. (2000)
object: Lindqvist et al. (2000) performed genome scans in families with multiple SLE patients from Iceland, a geographic and genetic isolate, and from Sweden. In the Icelandic families, 5 regions had lod scores greater than 2.0: 4p15-p13 (Z = 3.20), 9p22 (Z = 2.27), and 19q13 (Z = 2.06), which are homologous to the murine regions containing the lmb2, sle2, and sle3 loci, respectively; 19p13 (D19S247, Z = 2.58); and 2q37 (D2S125, Z = 2.06).

subject: Lindqvist et al. (2000)
object: In Swedish families with multiple SLE patients, Lindqvist et al. (2000) found only 2 regions with lod scores above 2.0: 2q11 (D2S436, Z = 2.13) and 2q37 (D2S125, Z = 2.18). Combining the Icelandic and Swedish family sets gave a highly significant lod score of 4.24 at D2S125 in favor of linkage to 2q37, which the authors concluded represents a new SLE susceptibility locus (hSLE1).

subject: Gaffney et al. (2000)
object: Gaffney et al. (2000) performed a second complete genome screen in a new cohort of 82 SLE sib-pair families (Minnesota cohort 2). The four best intervals were 7p22 (lod score 2.87), 7q21 (lod score 2.40), 10p13 (lod score 2.24), and 7q36 (lod score 2.15); 8 additional intervals had lod scores of 1.00-1.67.

subject: Gaffney et al. (2000)
object: In a combined analysis of Minnesota cohorts 1 and 2 (187 SLE sib-pair families), Gaffney et al. (2000) found significant linkage to markers in 6p11-p21 (D6S426, lod score 4.19) and 16q13 (D16S415, lod score 3.85). Three intervals (2p15, 7q36, and 1q42) had lod scores of 1.92-2.06, and 13 other intervals had lod scores of 1.00-1.78.

subject: Gross et al. (2000)
object: Gross et al. (2000) found that transgenic mice overexpressing zTNF4 (BLyS, BAFF, TALL-1, THANK), a member of the TNF ligand family, in lymphoid cells developed symptoms characteristic of SLE and had an expanded rare population of splenic B-1a lymphocytes. Circulating zTNF4 was also more abundant in NZBWF1 and MRL-lpr/lpr mice during the onset and progression of SLE.

subject: Gross et al. (2000)
object: Gross et al. (2000) identified 2 TNF receptor family members, TACI and BCMA, as receptors that bind zTNF4. The authors concluded that zTNF4 and its receptors are involved in the development of SLE.

subject: Gross et al. (2000)
object: Gross et al. (2000) showed that treating NZBWF1 lupus-prone mice with a soluble TACI-Ig fusion protein inhibited the development of proteinuria and prolonged survival. They suggested that TACI-Ig was a promising treatment for autoimmune disease in humans.

subject: Napirei et al. (2000)
object: Napirei et al. (2000) generated Dnase1-deficient mice by gene targeting and found that they showed classical symptoms of SLE, namely antinuclear antibodies, deposition of immune complexes in glomeruli, and full-blown glomerulonephritis, in a Dnase1-dose-dependent manner. The authors suggested that lack or reduction of Dnase1 is a critical factor in the initiation of human SLE.

subject: Napirei et al. (2000)
object: Napirei et al. (2000) found, in agreement with earlier reports, that serum DNASE1 activities were lower in SLE patients than in normal subjects.

subject: Gray-McGuire et al. (2000)
object: Gray-McGuire et al. (2000) performed a genome scan of 126 pedigrees multiplex for SLE, including 469 sibling pairs (affected and unaffected) and 175 affected relative pairs. They used revised multipoint Haseman-Elston regression and conditional logistic regression and identified a novel linkage to chromosome 4p16-15.2 (P = 0.0003 and lod = 3.84). They confirmed this linkage in European American families using an independent pedigree collection.

subject: Gray-McGuire et al. (2000)
object: Gray-McGuire et al. (2000) presented evidence of an epistatic interaction between chromosome 4p16-15.2 and chromosome 5p15 in their European American SLE families.

subject: Gray-McGuire et al. (2000)
object: Gray-McGuire et al. (2000) reported that their data supported the published results of 3 independent studies for 9 regions reported to be linked to SLE. Their data also agreed with earlier published results from a subset of the same data for 3 regions.

subject: Zhang et al. (2001)
object: Zhang et al. (2001) demonstrated significant elevations of B lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS) in sera of patients with SLE. BLyS isolated from SLE patient sera had the same molecular weight as the natural soluble form and stimulated B cell activation in vitro. The authors suggested that BLyS likely plays a critical role in triggering activation of self-antigen-driven autoimmune B cells in human SLE and may provide an effective therapeutic target.

subject: Zhang et al. (2001)
object: Zhang et al. (2001) found that increased BLyS in SLE patients was partially associated with higher levels of anti-dsDNA antibodies of the IgG, IgM, and IgA classes, but was not associated with disease activity; they suggested BLyS may be a useful marker for early activation of an autoimmune diathesis.

subject: Solomou et al. (2001)
object: Solomou et al. (2001) found that nuclear extracts from unstimulated SLE T cells, unlike those from normal T cells, contained increased amounts of phosphorylated cAMP-responsive element modulator (p-CREM), which bound the -180 site of the IL-2 promoter. After stimulation, normal T-cell extracts showed increased binding of phosphorylated CREB (p-CREB) to this site. Stimulated SLE T-cell extracts showed mainly p-CREM binding and less p-CREB binding. In SLE T cells, p-CREM bound the transcriptional coactivators CREB binding protein and p300.

subject: Solomou et al. (2001)
object: Solomou et al. (2001) found that higher p-CREM expression correlated with lower IL-2 production. A reporter gene driven by the IL-2 promoter -180 site was transcribed more strongly in normal T cells but was suppressed in SLE T cells. The authors concluded that transcriptional repression is responsible for the decreased IL-2 production by SLE T cells.

subject: Yasutomo et al. (2001)
object: Yasutomo et al. (2001) found a heterozygous nonsense mutation in exon 2 of the DNASE1 gene in 2 patients with systemic lupus erythematosus. The patients had decreased DNASE1 activity and an extremely high IgG titer against nucleosomal antigens. The authors concluded that the data were consistent with the hypothesis that low DNASE1 activity is directly connected to the progression of human SLE.

subject: DNASE1 heterozygous nonsense mutation in exon 2 of DNASE1
object: DNASE1

subject: Yasutomo et al. (2001)
object: Yasutomo et al. (2001) noted that mice deficient in Dnase1 develop an SLE-like syndrome.

subject: DeGiorgio et al. (2001)
object: DeGiorgio et al. (2001) noted that the pentapeptide Asp/Glu-Trp-Asp/Glu-Tyr-Ser/Gly, which they had previously shown to mimic double-stranded DNA, is also present in the extracellular domain of the murine and human NMDA receptor subunits NR2a and NR2b. They showed that both murine and human anti-DNA antibodies recognize the NR2 receptor, and that anti-DNA antibodies with this cross-reactivity mediate apoptotic death of neurons in vivo and in vitro.

subject: DeGiorgio et al. (2001)
object: DeGiorgio et al. (2001) found that the cerebrospinal fluid of a patient with SLE contained anti-DNA/NR2 cross-reactive antibodies and caused neuronal death through an apoptotic pathway. The authors concluded that lupus antibodies cross-react with DNA and NMDA receptors, get into the cerebrospinal fluid, and may mediate non-thrombotic and non-vasculitic CNS abnormalities.

subject: Blanco et al. (2001)
object: Blanco et al. (2001) found that blood monocytes from SLE patients functioned as antigen-presenting cells in vitro, and that SLE patient serum induced normal monocytes to differentiate into dendritic cells (DCs). These DCs could capture antigens from dying cells and present them to CD4-positive T cells.

subject: Blanco et al. (2001)
object: Blanco et al. (2001) showed that the capacity of SLE patient serum to induce DC differentiation correlated with disease activity and depended on interferon-alpha (IFN-alpha). They proposed that unabated induction of DCs by IFN-alpha may drive the autoimmune response in SLE.

subject: Stein et al. (2002)
object: Stein et al. (2002) analyzed 372 affected individuals from 160 multiplex SLE pedigrees, 25 of which contained at least 1 affected male relative. Renal disease was significantly more frequent in female family members with an affected male relative than in those without (68% vs 43%; P = 0.002), a trend that persisted after stratification by race and was most pronounced in European Americans.

subject: Stein et al. (2002)
object: Stein et al. (2002) concluded that the increased prevalence of renal disease previously reported in men with SLE is largely a familial rather than a sex-based difference, at least in multiplex SLE families. A familial basis for differences in hematologic and immunologic manifestations was also suggested, whereas arthritis and dermatologic features appeared most influenced by sex.

subject: Leadbetter et al. (2002)
object: Leadbetter et al. (2002) showed that rheumatoid factor (RF)-positive B cells were effectively activated by IgG2a-chromatin immune complexes. Activation required the antigen receptor and a member of the MyD88-dependent Toll-like receptor (TLR) family to be engaged together, and inhibitor studies implicated TLR9. The authors concluded that this links innate and adaptive immunity in the development of systemic autoimmune disease. They also said it explains why so many autoantibodies react with nucleic acid-protein particles.

subject: Kyogoku et al. (2002)
object: Kyogoku et al. (2002) screened FCGR2B for variants by direct sequencing and PCR-SSCP of cDNA and identified a SNP, c.695T>C, causing a nonsynonymous ile232-to-thr (I232T) substitution in the transmembrane domain. In 193 Japanese patients with SLE and 303 healthy controls, the frequency of the 232T/T genotype was significantly increased in patients, and the authors concluded that FCGR2B I232T is associated with susceptibility to SLE in the Japanese.

subject: FCGR2B c.695T>C / p.I232T
object: FCGR2B

subject: Kyogoku et al. (2002)
object: Kyogoku et al. (2002) genotyped the same 193 Japanese SLE patients and 303 controls for FCGR2A-131R/H, FCGR3A-176V/F, and FCGR3B-NA1/2 polymorphisms and found significant association of FCGR3A-176F/F with SLE. Two-locus analyses suggested that both FCGR2B and FCGR3A may contribute to SLE susceptibility, whereas the previously reported FCGR3B association was considered secondary, deriving from strong linkage disequilibrium with FCGR2B.

subject: FCGR3A FCGR3A-176F/F
object: FCGR3A

subject: Graham et al. (2002)
object: Graham et al. (2002) genotyped a dense map of polymorphic microsatellites across the HLA region in a large collection of SLE families and identified 3 distinct haplotypes spanning the class II region that showed transmission distortion. DRB1 and DQB1 typing of founders showed that these haplotypes carried DRB1*1501/DQB1*0602, DRB1*0801/DQB1*0402, and DRB1*0301/DQB1*0201, respectively. The authors concluded that HLA class II haplotypes containing DRB1 and DQB1 alleles are strong risk factors for human SLE.

subject: Graham et al. (2002)
object: By visualizing ancestral recombinants, Graham et al. (2002) narrowed the SLE-associated haplotypes containing DRB1*1501 and DRB1*0801 to a region of about 500 kb.

subject: Quintero-Del-Rio et al. (2002)
object: Quintero-Del-Rio et al. (2002) evaluated genome scan data from more than 300 microsatellite markers in 75 SLE pedigrees with at least 1 SLE patient meeting the ACR renal criterion. Parametric analysis gave a maximum screening lod score of 3.16 at 10q22.3 in European American pedigrees, and multipoint sib-pair regression analysis gave P = 0.0000008 at 10q22.3 in European Americans; this locus was designated SLEN1 and had not been previously described.

subject: Quintero-Del-Rio et al. (2002)
object: In the same 75 pedigrees, Quintero-Del-Rio et al. (2002) found a maximum screening lod score of 2.58 at 11p15.6 in African American pedigrees, and sib-pair regression analysis gave P = 0.000001 at 2q34-35 in African Americans (SLEN2). The 2q34-35 locus had not been previously described.

subject: Quintero-Del-Rio et al. (2002)
object: Quintero-Del-Rio et al. (2002) studied 35 pedigrees with 2 or more SLE patients with renal disease and found a lod score of 3.34 at 11p15.6 in African American pedigrees (SLEN3). Sib-pair analysis in these pedigrees also showed P = 0.00003 at 4q13.1 in European Americans, and P = 0.00003 at 11p13 and P = 0.00007 at 3q23 in African Americans. The authors concluded that multiple genetic linkages are related to the renal criterion in SLE.

subject: Quintero-Del-Rio et al. (2002)
object: Quintero-Del-Rio et al. (2002) noted that renal disease occurs in 40 to 75% of SLE patients and contributes significantly to morbidity and mortality.

subject: Kelly et al. (2002)
object: Kelly et al. (2002) noted that SLE shows familial aggregation, with lambda(s) estimates of 10 to 20 and a monozygotic twin concordance rate above 20.

subject: Kelly et al. (2002)
object: Kelly et al. (2002) reviewed completed linkage studies of pedigrees multiplex for SLE. These studies identified 60 susceptibility loci. Seven of them met or exceeded the threshold for significant linkage (LOD at least 3.3 or P at most 0.00005): 1q22-23, 1q41, 2q37, 4p16, 6p21-11, 16q13 and 17p13. Linkage at 1q41, 4p16 and 6p21 had been independently confirmed. For 1q22-23 and 2q37 there was additional suggestive evidence.

subject: Kelly et al. (2002)
object: Kelly et al. (2002) observed that the SLE linkages usually dominate in one ethnicity or another. They suggested that the responsible polymorphisms will also vary by ethnicity.

subject: Kelly et al. (2002)
object: Kelly et al. (2002) noted that SLE has known genetic associations at numerous candidate loci, including various HLA alleles, complement component genes and Fc-gamma receptors. Murine lupus models had provided additional candidate genes and potential syntenic linkages.

subject: Johanneson et al. (2002)
object: Johanneson et al. (2002) genotyped 87 multicase SLE families from European (Iceland, Sweden, England, Norway, Italy, and Greece) and recently admixed (Mexico, Colombia, and the United States) populations for 62 microsatellite markers on chromosome 1. Parametric two-point linkage analysis found 6 regions (1p36, 1p21, 1q23, 1q25, 1q31, and 1q43) with lod scores of 1.50 or higher, all previously described, with contributions differing by population of origin.

subject: Johanneson et al. (2002)
object: Johanneson et al. (2002) found a significant 3-point lod score of 3.79 at 1q31, contributed by families from all populations with several markers under the same parametric model, and concluded that this locus contains a major susceptibility gene important to SLE in general populations.

subject: Johanneson et al. (2002)
object: Johanneson et al. (2002) found that analysis of a known mutation in the CD45 gene did not support a role for this mutation in SLE.

subject: Prokunina et al. (2002)
object: Within the SLEB2 susceptibility locus, which they had previously identified in Nordic multi-case families, Prokunina et al. (2002) studied 2,510 individuals for SNPs they identified in PDCD1. The individuals came from 5 independent sets of families and also included unrelated individuals with SLE. One intronic SNP in PDCD1 was associated with SLE in Europeans: it was found in 12% of affected individuals versus 5% of controls (P = 0.00001, relative risk = 2.6). It was also associated with SLE in Mexicans, where it was found in 7% of affected individuals versus 2% of controls (P = 0.0009, relative risk = 3.5).

subject: PDCD1 intronic SNP in PDCD1
object: PDCD1

subject: Prokunina et al. (2002)
object: Prokunina et al. (2002) found that the SLE-associated allele of the intronic PDCD1 SNP alters a binding site for the transcription factor RUNX1 (AML1) in an intronic enhancer. They suggested that this is a mechanism by which the SNP could contribute to the development of SLE.

subject: Prokunina et al. (2002)
object: Prokunina et al. (2002) noted that they had previously reported a susceptibility locus, SLEB2, in Nordic multi-case SLE families. They regarded PDCD1 as the strongest candidate gene within that locus.

subject: Prokunina et al. (2002)
object: Prokunina et al. (2002) stated that SLE is a complex autoimmune disease that affects 0.05% of the Western population, mostly women.

subject: Sun et al. (2002)
object: Sun et al. (2002) found that treating Fas-deficient MRL/lpr mice with an agonistic monoclonal antibody to CD137 (2A) blocked lymphadenopathy and spontaneous autoimmune disease and led to prolonged survival. The 2A treatment quickly increased IFN-gamma production and depleted autoreactive B cells and abnormal double-negative T cells. The authors suggested this happened through increased apoptosis by Fas- and TNF receptor-independent mechanisms. They concluded that agonistic antibodies against costimulatory molecules might be used to delete autoreactive lymphocytes and block autoimmune disease progression.

subject: Scofield et al. (2003)
object: Scofield et al. (2003) selected 38 of 184 SLE-multiplex pedigrees that contained an SLE patient with thrombocytopenia (platelets less than 100,000/microL) and established linkage at 1q22-23 (maximum lod = 3.71) in these 38 pedigrees and at 11p13 (maximum lod = 5.72) in the 13 African American pedigrees among them.

subject: Scofield et al. (2003)
object: Scofield et al. (2003) found that in SLE multiplex pedigrees, thrombocytopenia was associated with nephritis, serositis, neuropsychiatric involvement, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, anti-double-stranded DNA, and antiphospholipid antibody, and that SLE was more severe in families with a thrombocytopenic SLE patient whether or not thrombocytopenia in an individual patient was considered. They concluded that thrombocytopenia is a component of a severe familial form of SLE.

subject: Molokhia et al. (2003)
object: Molokhia et al. (2003) studied 124 SLE cases and 219 matched controls living in Trinidad. They restricted the admixture analysis to 52 cases and 107 controls who reported no Indian or Chinese ancestry, and typed these individuals with 26 SNPs and 5 insertion/deletion polymorphisms that differ strongly in frequency between west African, European, and Native American populations. Mean west African admixture was 0.81 in cases and 0.74 in controls (P = 0.01). The risk ratio for SLE per unit change in admixture was 32.5 (95% CI 2.0-518), and adjusting for socioeconomic status changed it only slightly (28.4, 95% CI 1.7-485).

subject: Molokhia et al. (2003)
object: Molokhia et al. (2003) concluded that their results support an additive genetic model for the ethnic difference in SLE risk between west Africans and Europeans. They favored this over an environmental explanation or an 'overdominant' model, and stated that this lays a basis for localizing the responsible genes by admixture mapping.

subject: Baechler et al. (2003)
object: Baechler et al. (2003) used global gene expression profiling of peripheral blood mononuclear cells and identified distinct patterns of gene expression that distinguished most SLE patients from healthy controls. About half of the patients showed dysregulated expression of genes in the interferon (IFN) pathway. The authors suggested that these results gave insight into the genetic pathways underlying SLE.

subject: Baechler et al. (2003)
object: Baechler et al. (2003) found that the IFN gene expression signature marked more severe SLE involving the kidneys, hematopoietic cells, and/or the central nervous system. They suggested that it identified a subgroup of patients who might benefit from therapies targeting the IFN pathway.

subject: Nakamura et al. (2003)
object: Nakamura et al. (2003) carried out genome-wide scans in SLE-prone New Zealand Black (NZB) x New Zealand White (NZW) F1 (B/W F1) mice. They found that a region on NZB chromosome 4 that includes interferon-alpha (IFN-alpha) was significantly linked to anxiety-like behavior. Mice carrying heterozygous NZB/NZW alleles of this susceptibility region on the NZW background also showed anxiety-like behavior, which confirmed the linkage.

subject: Nakamura et al. (2003)
object: Nakamura et al. (2003) found that neuronal IFN-alpha and corticotropin-releasing hormone levels were higher in B/W F1 mice than in NZW mice. Blocking the mu-1 opioid receptor or corticotropin-releasing hormone receptor 1 partially overcame the anxiety-like behavior of B/W F1 mice. Pretreatment with a mu-1 opioid receptor antagonist abolished the anxiety-like behavior seen in IFN-alpha-treated NZW mice. The authors suggested that a genetically determined endogenous excess of IFN-alpha in the brain may form one aspect of the anxiety-like behavior seen in SLE-prone mice.

subject: Kamat et al. (2003)
object: Kamat et al. (2003) reported the first case of identical triplets who all developed systemic lupus erythematosus, diagnosed in reverse birth order at ages 8, 9, and 11 years. Although genetically identical, each sibling showed different clinical signs and symptoms, but all 3 had skin rash, fatigue, and biopsy-proven glomerulonephritis at different ages. Laboratory findings were similar, with positive antinuclear, anti-native DNA, and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies and low complement levels.

subject: Russell et al. (2004)
object: Russell et al. (2004) studied the CRP and APCS genes on 1q23.2 in 586 UK simplex SLE families (2 cohorts). Patients with SLE were more likely to inherit the minor A allele of CRP 4 (rs1205, G>A), a SNP in the 3-prime flanking/untranslated region of CRP. Transmission testing showed this (TRANSMIT P = 0.006 in 498 European-Caucasian families; P = 0.003 in all 586 families; P = 0.0008 in 394 trios).

subject: CRP CRP 4 (rs1205) G>A
object: CRP

subject: Russell et al. (2004)
object: Russell et al. (2004) found that the rare allele of CRP 4 was also linked with antinuclear autoantibody (ANA) production. In the combined cohorts, the rare allele was over-transmitted to ANA-positive individuals (P = 0.002). There was no association with renal lupus or with other autoantibodies.

subject: CRP CRP 4 rare allele
object: CRP

subject: Russell et al. (2004)
object: Russell et al. (2004) found that basal serum CRP levels were independently influenced by CRP 4 (P = 0.003) and by CRP 2 (rs1800947, a synonymous G>C change at codon 188; P = 0.01), and this held in both SLE patients and siblings. CRP haplotypes 2 and 5, which carry the CRP 4 minor allele, were associated with lower basal CRP. The authors suggested that reduced basal CRP expression predisposes to SLE, possibly by impairing clearance of cellular debris.

subject: CRP CRP 2 (rs1800947) G>C synonymous codon 188
object: CRP

subject: Li et al. (2004)
object: Li et al. (2004) carried out genome-wide scans for susceptibility genes for aberrant activation of self-reactive CD5+ B1 cells in SLE-prone New Zealand Black (NZB) mice and (NZB x NZW)F1 mice. They identified Ltk, which encodes leukocyte tyrosine kinase, as a possible candidate gene. Sequence and functional analyses showed that NZB mice carry a gain-of-function polymorphism in the LTK kinase domain near YXXM, the binding motif for the p85 subunit of PI3K.

subject: Li et al. (2004)
object: Li et al. (2004) found that SLE patients carried an LTK polymorphism of the same gain-of-function type as the one in NZB mice. Its frequency was significantly higher in patients than in healthy controls.

subject: Li et al. (2004)
object: Li et al. (2004) suggested that these polymorphic LTK proteins up-regulate the PI3K pathway. They proposed that this may be one genetic component of susceptibility to abnormal proliferation of self-reactive B cells in SLE.

subject: Xu et al. (2004)
object: Xu et al. (2004) used gene microarray profiling, checked by functional and biochemical studies, to show that activated T cells from SLE patients resisted anergy and apoptosis by strongly upregulating and sustaining COX-2 expression. Inhibiting COX-2 made these anergy-resistant lupus T cells undergo apoptosis by increasing Fas signaling and sharply lowering the survival molecule c-FLIP. The authors noted that the gene encoding COX-2 lies in a lupus-susceptibility region on chromosome 1.

subject: Xu et al. (2004)
object: Xu et al. (2004) used COX-2 inhibitors and Cox-2-deficient mice to confirm that the COX-2/FLIP antiapoptosis program was used selectively by anergy-resistant lupus T cells and not by cancer cells or other autoimmune T cells. Only some COX-2 inhibitors suppressed the production of pathogenic anti-DNA autoantibodies by causing autoimmune T-cell apoptosis, and this effect did not depend on PGE2.

subject: Tournoy et al. (2004)
object: Tournoy et al. (2004) found that mice heterozygous for Ps1 deficiency and homozygous for Ps2 deficiency (PS1+/-PS2-/-), which had considerably lowered PS1 protein, reduced gamma-secretase activity, and impaired beta-catenin downregulation, were normal up to about 6 months of age, when most developed an autoimmune disease with dermatitis, glomerulonephritis, keratitis, and vasculitis resembling human systemic lupus erythematosus. The mice showed B-cell dominated infiltrates, hypergammaglobulinemia with immune complex deposits in several tissues, high-titer nuclear autoantibodies, and an increased CD4+/CD8+ ratio. PS1+/-PS2+/- mice remained healthy, which the authors suggested pointed to a sharply defined minimum of presenilin function.

subject: Barreto et al. (2004)
object: Barreto et al. (2004) tested whether SLE was associated with 2 CTLA4 polymorphisms: an SNP at position +49 of exon 1 and a dinucleotide repeat in the 3-prime UTR. The 3-prime UTR repeat was significantly associated with SLE. One allele conferred susceptibility and another conferred protection. The authors said the associated alleles did not support an allele size-dependent effect of the repeat. Instead, they suggested that the repeat is in linkage disequilibrium with a true causative locus.

subject: CTLA4 dinucleotide repeat in the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR)
object: CTLA4

subject: Barreto et al. (2004)
object: Barreto et al. (2004) found no association between SLE and the CTLA4 exon 1 +49 SNP in their own population. Earlier studies had disagreed on this SNP, so they ran a meta-analysis of 7 published studies plus their own. In the meta-analysis, carriers of the G allele had a significantly increased risk of SLE and carriers of the A allele had a significantly decreased risk.

subject: CTLA4 single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in position +49 of exon 1
object: CTLA4

subject: Su et al. (2004)
object: Su et al. (2004) identified 10 novel SNPs in the promoter region of the FCGR2B gene, which defined two functionally distinct haplotypes in the proximal promoter. In a case-control study of 600 Caucasians, the less frequent FCGR2B promoter haplotype was significantly associated with SLE (odds ratio = 1.65; p = 0.0054). This haplotype was not in linkage disequilibrium with previously identified FCGR2A and FCGR3A polymorphisms, and the association remained after adjustment for them (odds ratio = 1.72; p = 0.0083).

subject: Su et al. (2004)
object: In luciferase reporter assays, Su et al. (2004) found that the less frequent FCGR2B promoter haplotype increased reporter gene expression in B lymphoid and myeloid cell lines under both constitutive and stimulated conditions. The authors suggested that an expression variant of FCGR2B is a risk factor for human lupus and implicated FCGR2B in disease pathogenesis.

subject: Kyogoku et al. (2004)
object: Kyogoku et al. (2004) genotyped 525 independent North American white individuals with SLE and 1,961 white controls for the PTPN22 R620W polymorphism. The SNP was associated with SLE (genotypic P = 0.00009), with minor T allele frequencies of 12.67% in cases and 8.64% in controls. One copy of the T allele (W620) increased SLE risk (OR = 1.37; 95% CI 1.07-1.75), and two copies more than doubled this risk (OR = 4.37; 95% CI 1.98-9.65).

subject: PTPN22 p.R620W
object: PTPN22

subject: Kyogoku et al. (2004)
object: Kyogoku et al. (2004) concluded that, together with association of the same PTPN22 SNP with type 1 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis, their data provided compelling evidence that PTPN22 plays a fundamental role in regulating the immune system and the development of autoimmunity.

subject: Shin et al. (2004)
object: Shin et al. (2004) identified 16 SNPs in DNase I (DNASE1) by direct sequencing and genotyped 6 of them in 350 Korean SLE patients and 330 controls. None was significantly associated with risk of SLE. However, the nonsynonymous exon 8 SNP +2373A>G (Gln244Arg) was significantly associated with production of anti-RNP and anti-dsDNA antibodies among SLE patients. Arg/Arg homozygosity was more frequent in patients with anti-RNP antibody than in those without it (31.3% vs 14.4%; P = 0.0006, OR = 2.86).

subject: DNASE1 p.Q244R
object: DNASE1

subject: Shin et al. (2004)
object: Shin et al. (2004) did not find the DNASE1 exon 2 A/T mutation, previously reported in 2 Japanese SLE patients, in any of 350 Korean SLE patients or 330 controls. Taken together with earlier reports, they concluded that this result strongly suggests the mutation is absent from Caucasian, African, and Asian populations.

subject: DNASE1 A/T mutation in exon 2
object: DNASE1

subject: Kozlowski et al. (2004)
object: Kozlowski et al. (2004) reported 2 brothers from Cape Town with chondrodysplasia punctata, diagnosed clinically and radiographically. The older brother was born in 1991 and the younger, more severely affected brother in 2000. Their mother had longstanding disseminated lupus erythematosus and epilepsy and was treated with chloroquine and other drugs during both pregnancies. The parents were not consanguineous and the family history was unremarkable.

subject: Kozlowski et al. (2004)
object: Kozlowski et al. (2004) noted that 7 earlier cases of chondrodysplasia punctata linked to maternal lupus erythematosus had been reported. They concluded that maternal lupus erythematosus must be regarded as another cause of chondrodysplasia punctata.

subject: Sigurdsson et al. (2005)
object: Sigurdsson et al. (2005) tested 44 SNPs in 13 type I interferon pathway genes for joint linkage and association with SLE. The study included 679 Swedish, Finnish and Icelandic patients with SLE, 798 unaffected family members and 438 unrelated controls. SNPs in the TYK2 and IRF5 genes gave strong signals in the joint analysis of linkage and association (unadjusted P less than 10(-7)).

subject: Sigurdsson et al. (2005)
object: Sigurdsson et al. (2005) noted that TYK2 binds to the type I interferon receptor complex and that IRF5 regulates type I interferon gene expression. They concluded that their association findings support an SLE disease mechanism involving key components of the type I interferon system.

subject: Tao et al. (2005)
object: Tao et al. (2005) found that NK T cells from patients with active SLE were highly sensitive to anti-CD95-induced apoptosis compared with those from normal subjects and inactive SLE patients, and that CD226 expression and expression of the antiapoptotic protein survivin were deficient in NK T cells from active SLE patients. CD226 preactivation significantly upregulated survivin expression and activation and rescued active SLE NK T cells from anti-CD95-induced apoptosis.

subject: Tao et al. (2005)
object: In transfected COS7 cells, Tao et al. (2005) showed that anti-CD95-mediated death signals were inhibited by activation of the CD226 pathway through stabilization of caspase-8 and caspase-3 and through activation of survivin. They concluded that deficient expression of CD226 and survivin in NK T cells from active SLE is a molecular basis of the high apoptotic sensitivity of these cells, offering a potential explanation for reduced NK T cell numbers in SLE.

subject: McGaha et al. (2005)
object: McGaha et al. (2005) showed that partially restoring levels of the inhibitory Fc receptor FcgRIIB on B cells in lupus-prone mouse strains was enough to restore tolerance and prevent autoimmunity. They concluded that FcgRIIB regulates a common B cell checkpoint in genetically diverse lupus-prone strains, and that modest changes in its expression can lead to either tolerance or autoimmunity. They suggested that increasing FcgRIIB levels on B cells may be an effective way to treat autoimmune diseases.

subject: Lee et al. (2005)
object: In a meta-analysis of 14 independent studies (to July 2004) testing association between CTLA4 polymorphisms (exon-1 +49, promoter -318 and -1722, and a 3-prime UTR dinucleotide repeat) and SLE, Lee et al. (2005) found that the CTLA4 exon-1 +49 polymorphism was significantly associated with SLE susceptibility; the overall odds ratio for the +49 GG genotype was 1.287 (95% CI 1.031-1.562, P = 0.011). The authors concluded that the +49 (A/G) polymorphism influences the risk of developing SLE, especially in Asians.

subject: CTLA4 exon-1 +49 (A/G)
object: CTLA4

subject: Lee et al. (2005)
object: Lee et al. (2005) found on ethnic stratification that the CTLA4 exon-1 +49 GG genotype was associated with SLE in Asians (OR 1.293, 95% CI 1.031-1.620, P = 0.026), with a similar but nonsignificant effect in European-derived populations (OR 1.268, P = 0.230). The +49 G risk allele was associated in Asians (OR 1.246, 95% CI 1.057-1.469, P = 0.009) but showed no allelic association in Europeans (OR 0.978, P = 0.780).

subject: CTLA4 exon-1 +49 risk allele (G)
object: CTLA4

subject: Blank et al. (2005)
object: Blank et al. (2005) identified a G-C substitution at position -343 relative to the transcription start site in the FCGR2B promoter (rs3219018). In European Americans, being homozygous for the C allele (-343 C/C) was associated with SLE (OR = 11.1, P = 0.003).

subject: FCGR2B -343 G/C (rs3219018)
object: FCGR2B

subject: Blank et al. (2005)
object: Blank et al. (2005) found that the -343 G-C substitution was associated with lower transcription from the FCGR2B promoter and reduced binding of the AP1 transcription complex to the variant promoter sequence. Activated B cells from SLE patients homozygous for -343 C/C had significantly reduced surface expression of FcgammaRIIb. The authors suggested that deregulated FCGR2B expression in -343 C/C homozygotes may play a role in the pathogenesis of SLE.

subject: FCGR2B -343 G/C
object: FCGR2B

subject: Barber et al. (2005)
object: Barber et al. (2005) examined the use of inhibitors of phosphoinositide 3-kinase gamma (PI3Kgamma), a lipid kinase that regulates inflammation, in the MRL-lpr mouse model of SLE. Treatment reduced glomerulonephritis and prolonged lifespan, suggesting that PI3Kgamma may be a useful target in the treatment of chronic inflammation.

subject: Floto et al. (2005)
object: Floto et al. (2005) showed that a recently described SLE-associated FcgammaRIIb polymorphism, FcgammaRIIb T232, which encodes a single amino acid substitution in the transmembrane domain, is functionally impaired. FcgammaRIIb T232 could not inhibit activatory receptors because it was excluded from sphingolipid rafts. The authors stated that this results in unopposed proinflammatory signaling, which is thought to promote SLE.

subject: FCGR2B FcgammaRIIbT(232)
object: FCGR2B

subject: Xing et al. (2005)
object: Xing et al. (2005) replicated, in a combined sample of 372 individuals from 159 families plus 392 individuals from 181 new families, the observation that SLE females with affected male relatives have a higher prevalence of renal disease than SLE females without affected male relatives, supporting the hypothesis that multiplex SLE families with at least one affected male ('male families') form a distinct subpopulation.

subject: Xing et al. (2005)
object: Xing et al. (2005) performed a genome-wide scan in 64 SLE multiplex families with affected male members and found the largest signal (lod = 3.08) at 13q32 in 18 African American male families using affected-relative-pair model-free linkage; IBD sharing suggested dominant inheritance, and multipoint model-based analysis gave a lod score of 3.13 (disease allele frequency 0.0004, penetrance 0.5). Fine mapping in these and 3 additional African American male families localized the locus to a region tightly linked to D13S892, confirming previously reported linkage of SLE to 13q32; the authors suggested the susceptibility gene is specific to African Americans with a form of SLE in which males are at high risk.

subject: Lee and Nath (2005)
object: Lee and Nath (2005) performed a genome search meta-analysis (GSMA) of 12 genome scan results from 9 independent studies, comprising 605 families with 1,355 SLE-affected individuals of Caucasian, African American, and Hispanic self-reported ethnicity. Two genomic locations, 6p22.3-6p21.1 (containing the HLA region) and 16p12.3-16q12.2, met genome-wide significance (p less than 0.000417), with clustering of significant adjacent bins on chromosomes 6 and 16.

subject: Lee and Nath (2005)
object: Lee and Nath (2005) found 12 additional bins with two pointwise p values less than 0.05, suggesting they likely contain SLE susceptibility loci, including 2 novel regions at 4q32.1-4q34.3 and 13q13.2-13q22.2.

subject: Lee and Nath (2005)
object: In a separate analysis restricted to Caucasian populations, Lee and Nath (2005) found the strongest evidence for linkage at 6p21.1-6q15 (Psumrnk = 0.00021), and suggested that a novel region at 3q22.1-3q25.33 (Psumrnk = 0.01376) may represent an ethnicity-specific SLE linkage.

subject: Lee et al. (2006)
object: Lee et al. (2006) performed a meta-analysis of 21 studies of the TNF-alpha promoter -308 A/G functional polymorphism and SLE.
