Overall, the A/A genotype was associated with SLE (OR 3.2, 95% CI 2.0-5.3, P less than 0.001), as were the A/A plus A/G genotypes (OR 2.0, CI 1.3-3.1, P less than 0.001). The authors concluded that the -308 A/G polymorphism may confer susceptibility to SLE, especially in European-derived populations.

subject: TNF -308 A/G promoter polymorphism
object: TNF

subject: Lee et al. (2006)
object: In ethnic stratification, Lee et al. (2006) found that the TNF -308 A/A genotype was associated with SLE in European-derived populations (OR 4.0, CI 2.5-6.4, P less than 0.001) but not in Asian-derived populations (OR 1.3, P = 0.76). The A allele was associated with SLE in Europeans (OR 2.1, CI 1.6-2.7, P less than 0.001). It was not associated in Asian (OR 1.4, P = 0.2) or African (OR 1.2, P = 0.59) populations.

subject: Aitman et al. (2006)
object: Aitman et al. (2006) found that, in humans, low copy number of FCGR3B, an orthologue of rat Fcgr3, was associated with glomerulonephritis in systemic lupus erythematosus.

subject: Aitman et al. (2006)
object: Aitman et al. (2006) used positional cloning in Wistar Kyoto rats to identify loss of a newly described rat-specific Fcgr3 paralogue, Fcgr3-related sequence (Fcgr3-rs), as a determinant of macrophage overactivity and immunologically mediated glomerulonephritis. They concluded that gene copy number polymorphism predisposes to immunologically mediated renal disease in two mammalian species.

subject: Graham et al. (2006)
object: Graham et al. (2006) replicated association of the IRF5 rs2004640 T allele with SLE in 4 independent case-control cohorts (P = 4.4 x 10(-16)) and by family-based transmission disequilibrium test analysis (P = 0.0006).

subject: IRF5 rs2004640 T allele
object: IRF5

subject: Graham et al. (2006)
object: Graham et al. (2006) found that the IRF5 rs2004640 T allele creates a 5-prime donor splice site in an alternate exon 1 (exon 1B), allowing expression of several unique IRF5 isoforms. They also identified an independent cis-acting variant, linked to the exon 1B splice site, associated with elevated IRF5 expression; haplotypes carrying the elevated-expression variant but lacking the exon 1B donor site did not confer SLE risk. They concluded that a common IRF5 haplotype driving elevated expression of multiple unique isoforms is an important genetic risk factor for SLE, establishing a causal role for type I IFN pathway genes in human autoimmunity.

subject: Kowal et al. (2006)
object: Kowal et al. (2006) found that serum from lupus patients that reacted with both DNA and the NMDA receptor (NMDAR) caused cognitive impairment in mice. The serum was given intravenously, and the mice also received lipopolysaccharide to break down the blood-brain barrier. The mice showed hippocampal neuron damage on histopathology and hippocampus-dependent memory impairment on behavioral testing.

subject: Kowal et al. (2006)
object: Kowal et al. (2006) eluted IgG from the brain of a lupus patient. This IgG bound DNA and NMDAR and caused neuronal apoptosis when injected into mouse brains. In the brains of 4 more patients with neuropsychiatric lupus, endogenous IgG colocalized with anti-NMDAR antibodies. The authors concluded that lupus patients have circulating anti-NMDAR antibodies that can cause neuronal damage and memory deficits if they cross the blood-brain barrier, and that these antibodies are present in patients' brains.

subject: Wu et al. (2007)
object: In a targeted genome scan of 1q21-43 in 126 lupus multiplex families containing 151 affected sib pairs, Wu et al. (2007) found evidence of linkage of SLE at 1q32.2 (nonparametric linkage score 2.52, P = 0.006).

subject: Wu et al. (2007)
object: Wu et al. (2007) analyzed 1,416 individuals from 258 Caucasian and 142 Chinese lupus simplex families and found that a common 3-SNP haplotype of the CR2 gene (rs3813946, rs1048971, rs17615) was associated with SLE susceptibility (P = 0.00001), conferring a 1.54-fold increased risk of disease. They concluded that CR2, a positional candidate at 1q32.2 and also a candidate in the murine Sle1c locus, is a likely SLE susceptibility gene.

subject: CR2 rs3813946
object: CR2

subject: CR2 rs1048971
object: CR2

subject: CR2 rs17615
object: CR2

subject: Wu et al. (2007)
object: Wu et al. (2007) found that SNP1 (rs3813946), located in the 5-prime untranslated region of CR2, altered transcriptional activity, suggesting a potential mechanism by which CR2 could contribute to the development of lupus.

subject: Yang et al. (2007)
object: Yang et al. (2007) studied C4 gene copy-number variation in 1,241 European Americans, including patients with SLE, their first-degree relatives, and unrelated healthy subjects, using definitive genotyping and phenotyping techniques. Compared with healthy subjects, patients with SLE had total C4 and C4A gene copy numbers shifted to the lower side. Having only 2 copies of total C4 significantly raised SLE risk (patients 9.3% vs unrelated controls 1.5%; OR = 6.514; P = 0.00002). Having 5 or more copies lowered the risk (5.79% vs 12%; OR = 0.466; P = 0.016).

subject: Yang et al. (2007)
object: Yang et al. (2007) found that having zero copies of C4A (OR = 5.267; P = 0.001) or one copy of C4A (OR = 1.613; P = 0.022) was a risk factor for SLE. Having 3 or more copies of C4A appeared to be protective (OR = 0.574; P = 0.012).

subject: Yang et al. (2007)
object: Among European Americans, Yang et al. (2007) found that gene copy number ranged from 2 to 6 for total C4, 0 to 5 for C4A, and 0 to 4 for C4B. Four copies of total C4, 2 of C4A, and 2 of C4B were the most common counts, but each made up only one-half to three-quarters of the study populations. Long C4 genes correlated with C4A (R = 0.695) and short C4 genes correlated with C4B (R = 0.437).

subject: Yang et al. (2007)
object: Using family-based association tests, Yang et al. (2007) suggested that a specific haplotype carrying a single short C4B gene was more likely to be passed to patients with SLE. This haplotype was in tight linkage disequilibrium with the -308A allele of TNFA.

subject: TNF -308A allele of TNFA
object: TNF

subject: Fanciulli et al. (2007)
object: Fanciulli et al. (2007) confirmed and strengthened an association between low FCGR3B copy number and SLE with glomerulonephritis (P = 1.4 x 10(-8)) in 161 UK SLE patients with glomerulonephritis compared with 312 controls from the UK 1958 birth cohort. Individuals with fewer than 2 copies of FCGR3B had a significantly higher risk of glomerulonephritis than those with 2 copies (OR = 2.43, P = 1 x 10(-3)).

subject: Fanciulli et al. (2007)
object: Fanciulli et al. (2007) found a strong association between FCGR3B copy number and SLE without known renal involvement in 375 unrelated UK cases (P = 1.4 x 10(-5)), with increased risk of SLE in individuals with fewer than 2 FCGR3B copies (OR = 2.21, P = 3 x 10(-4)). Across all 536 SLE cases, the P value of association was 2.7 x 10(-8). Among SLE patients, fewer than 2 copies did not significantly increase the risk of glomerulonephritis (OR = 1.09, P = 0.660).

subject: Fanciulli et al. (2007)
object: Fanciulli et al. (2007) observed zero copies of FCGR3B, indicating complete FCGR3B deficiency, in 25 of 1,279 (2%) individuals with autoimmunity, including 7 SLE patients with glomerulonephritis and 14 with SLE without nephritis. Only 1 of 862 controls (0.1%) had zero copies. The authors suggested that complete FCGR3B deficiency confers a very high risk of autoimmunity, particularly SLE.

subject: FCGR3B zero copies of FCGR3B
object: FCGR3B

subject: Fanciulli et al. (2007)
object: Fanciulli et al. (2007) also found association of low FCGR3B copy number with Wegener granulomatosis in UK (P = 3 x 10(-3)) and French (P = 1.1 x 10(-4)) cohorts, and with microscopic polyangiitis (P = 2.9 x 10(-4)). They found no association with the organ-specific diseases Graves disease (P = 0.65) or Addison disease (P = 0.057). This suggested different roles for FCGR3B copy number variation in systemic and organ-specific autoimmunity.

subject: Fanciulli et al. (2007)
object: Fanciulli et al. (2007) noted that FCGR3B is expressed by neutrophils and eosinophils and is important in tethering neutrophils to immune complexes and in clearing immune complexes. They hypothesized that in SLE, reduced clearance of immune complexes predisposes to disease in the glomeruli and at other sites.

subject: Lee-Kirsch et al. (2007)
object: Lee-Kirsch et al. (2007) found monoallelic frameshift or missense mutations, plus one 3-prime UTR variant, in the TREX1 gene in 9 of 417 individuals with systemic lupus erythematosus. None of these variants were found in 1,712 controls (P = 4.1 x 10(-7)). The authors concluded that TREX1 is implicated in the pathogenesis of SLE.

subject: Lee-Kirsch et al. (2007)
object: Lee-Kirsch et al. (2007) showed that 2 mutant TREX1 alleles found in SLE patients changed the subcellular targeting of the protein. They noted that TREX1 works together with the SET complex in granzyme A-mediated apoptosis.

subject: Remmers et al. (2007)
object: Remmers et al. (2007) tested SNPs in candidate genes in the previously linked chromosome 2q region. They then tested implicated STAT4 SNPs in 1,039 patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and 1,248 controls from 3 SLE case series. The haplotype marked by rs7574865 in intron 3 of STAT4 was strongly associated with lupus. It was present on 31% of chromosomes from patients and 22% from controls (P = 1.87 x 10(-9); odds ratio 1.55).

subject: STAT4 rs7574865
object: STAT4

subject: Remmers et al. (2007)
object: Remmers et al. (2007) found that being homozygous for the STAT4 risk allele, compared with not carrying it, was associated with more than double the risk of lupus. The same comparison showed a 60% increased risk of rheumatoid arthritis. The authors suggested that SLE and rheumatoid arthritis share a pathway.

subject: STAT4 rs7574865 risk allele
object: STAT4

subject: Kamatani et al. (2008)
object: Kamatani et al. (2008) ran a case-control association study using genome-wide gene-based SNP markers in 178 Japanese SLE patients and 899 controls. They found a significant association between SLE and SNP rs3130342, located in the 5-prime flanking region of the TNXB gene (P = 0.000000930; OR 3.11, 95% CI 1.89-5.28). The association was replicated in an independent set of 203 cases and 294 controls (P = 0.0440; OR 1.52, 95% CI 1.01-2.78). The authors concluded that TNXB is a candidate SLE susceptibility gene in the Japanese population.

subject: TNXB rs3130342
object: TNXB

subject: Kamatani et al. (2008)
object: Kamatani et al. (2008) found that the association of copy number variation (CNV) of the C4 gene, which lies next to TNXB, with SLE was weaker than the association of TNXB SNP rs3130342. They suggested that the C4 CNV association probably reflected linkage disequilibrium with this SNP. Stratified analysis showed that the rs3130342 association was independent of the HLA-DRB1*1501 allele.

subject: Cunninghame Graham et al. (2008)
object: Cunninghame Graham et al. (2008) genotyped 36 SNPs across TNFSF4 and 4 across TNFRSF4 in 416 UK European Caucasian SLE parental-affected trios and found, by TDT and haplotype-TDT analysis, association of the upstream region of TNFSF4 (gene-wide permuted P = 0.0020), with no association of TNFRSF4. A single overtransmitted upstream risk haplotype (haplotype 4), tagged by minor alleles of rs10912580, rs12039904, rs2205960 and rs1234317, was found in the UK (P = 0.0104) and replicated in 263 Minnesota trios (P = 3.00 x 10(-4)); an undertransmitted protective haplotype (haplotype 3) was tagged by the rare A allele of rs844644.

subject: TNFSF4 rs12039904
object: TNFSF4

subject: TNFSF4 rs844644
object: TNFSF4

subject: TNFSF4 rs10912580
object: TNFSF4

subject: TNFSF4 rs2205960
object: TNFSF4

subject: TNFSF4 rs1234317
object: TNFSF4

subject: Cunninghame Graham et al. (2008)
object: In a joint analysis of 778 UK and Minnesota trios, Cunninghame Graham et al. (2008) found the overtransmitted haplotype 4 (T/U 1.61) and undertransmitted haplotype 3 (T/U 0.73) remained significant after permutation (P < 1 x 10(-5)). Association was replicated in an independent case-control set of 424 UK SLE cases and 642 British 1958 Birth Cohort controls (rs2205960 OR 1.28; rs844644 OR 0.710, P = 6.83 x 10(-5)); combining all data, the strongest associations were rs12039904 (P = 1.91 x 10(-6)) and rs844644 (P = 6.08 x 10(-7)).

subject: Cunninghame Graham et al. (2008)
object: Conditional logistic regression by Cunninghame Graham et al. (2008) showed that the effect of each individual SNP disappeared when conditioned on haplotype background, supporting the hypothesis that no single genotyped variant was responsible for the upstream association, with the exception of rs844644 (P = 0.015). The T allele of rs1234317, which uniquely tags the risk haplotype, was predicted to destroy a binding site for the transcriptional repressor E4BP4.

subject: TNFSF4 rs1234317 T allele
object: TNFSF4

subject: Cunninghame Graham et al. (2008)
object: Cunninghame Graham et al. (2008) found in UK SLE families that TNFSF4 risk-haplotype tagging SNPs did not influence the lupus phenotype toward antiphospholipid syndrome, Sjogren syndrome, or lupus nephritis subtypes.

subject: Cunninghame Graham et al. (2008)
object: Cunninghame Graham et al. (2008) showed that activated lymphoblastoid cell lines homozygous for the overtransmitted TNFSF4 upstream haplotype had more TNFSF4-positive cells (P = 0.02) and a 6.7-fold increase in TNFSF4 transcript (P = 0.008) compared with lines homozygous for the undertransmitted haplotype; activated peripheral blood lymphocytes from 8 SLE probands showed consistent increased surface TNFSF4 with the risk haplotype. They hypothesized that increased TNFSF4 expression predisposes to SLE by augmenting T cell-APC interaction via TNFRSF4 co-stimulation.

subject: Balada et al. (2008)
object: Balada et al. (2008) measured the deoxymethylcytosine (dmC) content of DNA from purified CD4+ T cells by ELISA in 29 SLE patients and 30 healthy controls. Patients had significantly lower CD4+ T-cell DNA dmC content than controls (0.802 +/- 0.134 vs 0.901 +/- 0.133; P = 0.007), which fits with global DNA hypomethylation in SLE.

subject: Balada et al. (2008)
object: Balada et al. (2008) used real-time RT-PCR to measure DNMT1, DNMT3A and DNMT3B transcript levels in CD4+ T cells and found no difference between SLE patients and controls. However, low complement together with lymphopenia, high anti-dsDNA titers, or a SLEDAI score above 5 was associated with increased expression of at least one of the three methyltransferases. The authors suggested that patients with active disease might be responding indirectly to an underlying DNA hypomethylation by raising methyltransferase mRNA levels.

subject: Hom et al. (2008)
object: Hom et al. (2008) genotyped more than 500,000 SNPs in 1,311 patients with SLE and 1,783 controls, all North Americans of European descent, plus genotypes from 1,557 more controls taken from public repositories. They replicated the top loci in 793 patients and 857 controls from Sweden. Variation upstream of the transcription start sites of BLK and C8orf13 on chromosome 8p23.1 was associated with SLE in both the US and Swedish series (rs13277113; odds ratio, 1.39; P = 1 x 10(-10)).

object: International Consortium for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Genetics (SLEGEN) et al. (2008) found that the strongest association with SLE was in the HLA region at 6p21.3. subject: International Consortium for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Genetics (SLEGEN) et al. (2008)
object: International Consortium for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Genetics (SLEGEN) et al. (2008) found association between SLE and 3 markers spanning 149 kb in the IRF5 and TNPO3 region on 7q32. object: International Consortium for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Genetics (SLEGEN) et al. (2008) tested 20 previously reported associations with SLE or other autoimmune diseases in their genome-wide association data. They replicated the associations in PTPN22, FCGR2A and STAT4.

(2008) dropped the requirement for replication in every sample set and found additional possible non-HLA associations. These included markers in genomic regions containing XKR6, LYN, ATG5, ICA1, BLK and SCUBE1.

subject: International Consortium for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Genetics (SLEGEN) et al. (2008)
object: International Consortium for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Genetics (SLEGEN) et al. (2008) used stepwise logistic regression and found independent contributions from 2 HLA effects and 1 effect in each of 5 other regions. Considered jointly, these SNPs predicted SLE with a C statistic of 0.67 and explained about 15% of the sibling risk ratio of 29. The authors found no evidence of statistical interaction among the associated SNPs.

subject: Kozyrev et al. (2008)
object: In a genome-wide association scan using 85,042 SNPs, Kozyrev et al. (2008) identified an association between SLE and a nonsynonymous substitution in the BANK1 gene (rs10516487, R61H). The association was replicated in 4 independent case-control sets (combined P = 3.7 x 10(-10); OR = 1.38).

subject: Oishi et al. (2008)
object: Oishi et al. (2008) carried out a case-control association study in Japanese people using genome-wide gene-based SNPs. subject: Oishi et al. (2008)
object: Oishi et al. (2008) found that an SNP in NKX2.5 was also associated with SLE in Japanese people (P = 0.0037; odds ratio, 1.74; 95% CI, 1.19-2.55). Individuals with risk genotypes at both the ITPR3 and NKX2.5 loci had a higher risk of SLE (odds ratio, 5.77). The authors concluded that genetic and functional interactions between ITPR3 and NKX2.5 play a crucial role in SLE pathogenesis.

object: Oishi et al. (2008) found that the ITPR3 SNP rs3748079 was also associated with rheumatoid arthritis (P = 0.0084; odds ratio, 1.23) and with Graves disease (P = 0.00036; odds ratio, 1.57) in Japanese people.

subject: Willcocks et al. (2008)
object: Willcocks et al. (2008) confirmed an association between low FCGR3B copy number and SLE in a UK Caucasian population. They measured copy number by quantitative PCR in 171 patients and 176 ethnically matched controls (P = 0.027). They found no such association in a Hong Kong Chinese cohort of 159 cases and 150 controls, and none when the 57 patients with lupus nephritis were analyzed separately.

subject: Willcocks et al. (2008)
object: Willcocks et al. (2008) identified a woman with SLE whose neutrophils had no FCGR3 mRNA and no surface FcγRIIIb. Her monocytes had normal FCGR3 mRNA levels. Her son, daughter and one brother each carried one FCGR3B-null allele, showing Mendelian inheritance of the null allele. PCR showed that the deletion removed FCGR3B, HSPA7 and FCGR2C but spared FCGR3A and FCGR2B. CD59 was still expressed on neutrophils, which excluded a general defect in GPI anchoring.

object: In the FcγRIIIb-deficient family, Willcocks et al. (2008) found that FCGR3B copy number correlated with neutrophil adherence to IgG-coated surfaces under flow, immune complex binding and uptake, and serum levels of soluble FcγRIIIb. Superoxide production in response to stimuli thought to be Fc receptor–independent was not affected by copy number.

subject: Willcocks et al. (2008)
object: In 33 healthy individuals, Willcocks et al. (2008) found that FCGR3B copy number was associated with neutrophil FcγRIIIb expression, immune complex uptake and soluble FcγRIIIb levels. Individuals with high copy number showed 4 times the rate of neutrophil adherence to IgG-coated surfaces seen in those with low copy number. The authors suggested that low FCGR3B copy number predisposes to SLE through impaired neutrophil trafficking to inflammatory lesions and reduced immune complex clearance.

subject: Willcocks et al. (2008)
object: Willcocks et al. (2008) found that, unlike SLE, ANCA-associated systemic vasculitis was associated with high FCGR3B copy number (P = 10(-8)) in 556 patients from 3 UK cohorts compared with 286 controls. When tested directly on the same plate, patients with SLE had a significantly lower FCGR3B/CD36 ratio than patients with vasculitis (P = 0.0028).

subject: Graham et al. (2008)
object: Graham et al. (2008) performed a genome-wide association study of 311,238 SNPs in 431 unrelated SLE cases and 2,155 controls. Three regions reached genome-wide significance: HLA, IRF5/TNPO3, and a new SLE locus on chromosome 6q23 within the TNFAIP3 gene. The TNFAIP3 variant rs5029939 had a GWAS P value of 2.55 x 10(-8) and an odds ratio of 2.28. The association replicated in 740 independent trios (P = 2.47 x 10(-5)), giving a meta-analysis P value of 2.89 x 10(-12).

(2008) found that the minor alleles of the noncoding SNPs rs13192841 (OR 0.72, P = 7.9 x 10(-6)) and rs6922466 (OR 0.76, P = 0.00039) were protective. The authors concluded that, although some of the rs2230926 signal may reflect substructure within the European population, a signal remained after controlling for it.

subject: Musone et al. (2008)
object: Musone et al. (2008) reported that the coding SNP rs2230926 in TNFAIP3 causes a phe127-to-cys (F127C) change in A20. The risk cys127 protein was as stable as the phe127 protein. However, it was modestly but consistently less effective at inhibiting TNF-induced NF-kappa-B activity, which the authors suggested makes it a hypomorphic A20 protein.

subject: Musone et al. (2008)
object: Musone et al. (2008) suggested that TNFAIP3 polymorphisms may reduce the expression or anti-inflammatory activity of A20, which restricts NF-kappa-B signaling, and so predispose to SLE. They concluded that TNFAIP3 may be an important determinant of multiple autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis.

subject: Orrú et al. (2009)

object: Orrú et al. (2009) showed that the R263Q substitution in the catalytic domain of the lymphoid tyrosine phosphatase LYP, encoded by PTPN22, reduced phosphatase activity, and high-resolution structural analysis revealed the molecular basis for this loss of function. This contrasts with the gain-of-function R620W polymorphism, which is a risk factor for autoimmunity. The authors suggested that inhibiting LYP activity could be beneficial in human autoimmunity.

subject: Sthoeger et al. (2009)
object: Sthoeger et al. (2009) found that the mean serum level of alpha-defensin human neutrophil peptide-1 (HNP-1) in SLE patients (11.07 +/- 13.92 ng/microl) was significantly higher than in healthy controls (0.12 +/- 0.07 ng/microl). Sixty percent of patients had very high serum levels, and 50% showed increased alpha-defensin gene expression in polymorphonuclear cells. High alpha-defensin levels correlated with disease activity but not with neutrophil count. In contrast, beta-defensin-2 (hBD-2) could not be detected by ELISA, and its mRNA levels were low and similar to those in controls.

subject: Sthoeger et al. (2009)
object: Sthoeger et al. (2009) concluded that activation and degranulation of neutrophils led to alpha-defensin secretion in SLE patients. Because alpha-defensins have immunomodulatory effects, the authors suggested that their secretion may activate the adaptive immune system and lead to a systemic response.

subject: Sánchez et al. (2009)
object: Sánchez et al. (2009) genotyped 9 SNPs in the IL18 gene in Spanish SLE cases and controls. Two SNPs stayed significant after fine mapping. The SNP that survived correction for multiple testing, rs360719, was then genotyped in replication cohorts from Italy and Argentina. Its C allele remained associated with SLE across the sets and in the meta-analysis (pooled OR = 1.37, 95% CI 1.21-1.54, combined P = 3.8 x 10(-7)).

object: Sánchez et al. (2009) used quantitative real-time PCR to measure IL18 mRNA in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). IL18 mRNA levels were significantly higher in people carrying the rs360719 C risk allele. Electrophoretic mobility shift assays showed that this allele creates a binding site for the transcription factor OCT-1. The authors suggested that rs360719 may help determine SLE susceptibility and may be a key factor in IL18 expression.

subject: Han et al. (2009)
object: Han et al. (2009) performed a genome-wide association study of SLE in a Chinese Han population. They genotyped 1,047 cases and 1,205 controls with Illumina Human610-Quad BeadChips and replicated 78 SNPs in two additional cohorts (3,152 cases and 7,050 controls). They identified 9 new susceptibility loci, at ETS1, IKZF1, RASGRP3, SLC15A4, TNIP1, 7q11.23, 10q11.22, 11q23.3, and 16p11.2, with combined P values from 1.77 x 10(-25) to 2.77 x 10(-8).

subject: Han et al. (2009)
object: In the same Chinese Han study, Han et al. (2009) confirmed previously reported SLE susceptibility loci at BLK, IRF5, STAT4, TNFAIP3, TNFSF4, 6q21, and 22q11.21, with combined P values from 5.17 x 10(-42) to 5.18 x 10(-12).

subject: Han et al. (2009)
object: Han et al. (2009) compared their results with previous GWAS findings. They concluded that the comparison highlighted genetic heterogeneity in SLE susceptibility between Chinese Han and European populations.

subject: Gateva et al. (2009)
object: Gateva et al. (2009) selected SNPs from 2,466 regions that showed nominal association with SLE (P < 0.05) in a genome-wide scan of 1,310 cases and 7,859 controls. They genotyped these SNPs with a custom array in independent case-control samples from the United States (1,129 cases, 2,991 controls) and Sweden (834 cases, 1,338 controls). The study identified five new SLE susceptibility loci at genome-wide significance (P < 5 x 10(-8)): TNIP1 (OR = 1.27), PRDM1 (OR = 1.20), JAZF1 (OR = 1.20), UHRF1BP1 (OR = 1.17) and IL10 (OR = 1.19).

subject: Gateva et al. (2009)
object: Gateva et al. (2009) found that a SNP on 5q33.1 (rs7708392), located within an intron of TNIP1, was significantly associated with SLE in all three cohorts (combined P = 3.8 x 10(-13); OR 1.27). This SLE signal was 21 kb from, and appeared distinct from (r2 = 0.001), the psoriasis risk variants near TNIP1. The authors noted that TNIP1 interacts with TNFAIP3.

object: Gateva et al. (2009) tested 25 SNPs from 23 previously reported SLE loci and found further evidence of association for 21 of them. object: Willcocks et al. (2010) found that an FCGR2B SNP that abrogates the function of the inhibitory receptor FcgammaRIIb was strongly associated with susceptibility to SLE in both Caucasians and Southeast Asians.

subject: Willcocks et al. (2010)
object: Willcocks et al. (2010) found that the minor allele of the defunctioning FCGR2B SNP was more common in Southeast Asians and Africans, who live in areas where malaria is endemic, than in Caucasians. In an East African population, homozygosity for the minor allele was associated with substantial protection against severe malaria (odds ratio = 0.56; P = 7.1 x 10(-5)). The authors suggested that this protection may contribute to the higher frequency of the SNP, and therefore of SLE, in Africans and Southeast Asians.

subject: Niederer et al. (2010)
object: Niederer et al. (2010) used a triple paralogue ratio test (PRT) assay to measure FCGR3B copy number in Caucasian SLE cohorts from the UK and Sweden and their controls. Combined by meta-analysis, the two cohorts showed a significant association between low FCGR3B copy number (0 or 1 copies) and SLE (OR 1.57, 95% CI 1.08-2.27; P = 0.018). High copy number was not associated with SLE.

subject: Niederer et al. (2010)
object: In a Hong Kong Chinese SLE case-control cohort, Niederer et al. (2010) found a strong association between low FCGR3B copy number and SLE (OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.25-2.18; P = 4 x 10(-4)). The association was strongest in patients with lupus nephritis. Across all cohorts, the combined meta-analysis OR was 1.62 (95% CI 1.30-2.03). FCGR3A copy number did not differ between cases and controls.

subject: Niederer et al. (2010)
object: Niederer et al. (2010) genotyped 2 new Caucasian SLE cohorts from the UK and Sweden and confirmed that homozygosity for the FcgammaRIIB-232T allele (I232T, rs1050501) is associated with SLE. A meta-analysis of all Caucasian studies gave an OR of 2.26 (95% CI 1.49-3.41). In the Hong Kong Chinese cohort, 232T homozygotes showed a nonsignificant trend toward increase in SLE.

subject: Niederer et al. (2010)
object: Niederer et al. (2010) found weak-to-moderate linkage disequilibrium between FCGR3B copy number and FCGR2B I232T in Caucasian and Chinese controls. Low FCGR3B copy number was more common in carriers of the 232T allele. In logistic regression, however, FCGR3B copy number remained significant after adjusting for FCGR2B I232T in both populations (Chinese OR 1.67; Caucasian OR 1.55). The authors concluded that, despite the LD, the two variants have independent effects on SLE risk.

subject: Niederer et al. (2010)
object: Niederer et al. (2010) found that homozygosity for FcgammaRIIA-131R was more frequent in the SLE cohorts (OR 1.3 in both Chinese and Caucasians), but the association was not significant. FcgammaRIIIA V176F was not significantly associated with SLE.

subject: Niederer et al. (2010)
object: Niederer et al. (2010) suggested that the strong association between low FCGR3B copy number and SLE points to a role for neutrophils in protection from SLE. Their proposed mechanism is that reduced FcgammaRIIIB expression lowers immune complex uptake by neutrophils, leading to more immune complex deposition and inflammatory damage.

subject: Niederer et al. (2010)
object: Niederer et al. (2010) found significant ethnic differences in FCGR3B copy number. Low copy number was least common in Caucasians (7.4%), intermediate in Chinese and Vietnamese, and most common in Kenyans. High copy number was most common in Chinese and Vietnamese. FCGR3B copy number showed no association with ANCA-associated vasculitis, severe malaria, or bacterial sepsis.

subject: Olsson et al. (2012)
object: Olsson et al. (2012) found that patients with rheumatoid arthritis were less likely than controls to carry an increased copy number of NCF1 (7.6% vs 11.6%; p = 0.037). They suggested that an increased NCF1 copy number may protect against developing RA.

subject: Olsson et al. (2012)
object: Olsson et al. (2012) showed that the T allele of the NCF1-339 SNP (rs13447) is expressed from NCF1 and significantly reduces production of reactive oxygen species.

subject: NCF1 NCF1-339 (rs13447) T-allele
object: NCF1

subject: Boteva et al. (2012)
object: Boteva et al. (2012) genotyped 2,207 subjects of northern and southern European ancestry (1,028 SLE cases and 1,179 controls) from the UK and Spain. They measured total C4, C4A, and C4B gene copy numbers and the loss-of-function C4 exon 29 CT indel. Using multiple logistic regression with HLA-DRB1 and MHC region SNPs, they showed that genetically determined partial C4 deficiency states were not independent risk factors for SLE. The C4A exon 29 CT insertion was not associated with SLE in either cohort.

subject: C4A C4A exon 29 CT insertion
object: C4A

subject: Boteva et al. (2012)
object: Boteva et al. (2012) concluded that complete homozygous C4 deficiency is one of the strongest genetic risk factors for SLE. Partial C4 deficiency states, however, did not independently predispose to the disease. The authors suggested that earlier reported associations may reflect long-range linkage disequilibrium within the MHC.

subject: Manjarrez-Orduño et al. (2012)
object: Manjarrez-Orduño et al. (2012) found that SNPs tagging a CSK haplotype 'B' were nominally associated with SLE in a prior European GWAS (1,311 cases, 3,340 controls). Sequencing of CSK exons and conserved intronic regions in 24 European SLE patients homozygous for haplotype B identified the minor A allele of intronic SNP rs34933034 (G>A) on 34 of 48 B chromosomes. Genotyping of 3,769 SLE cases and 3,404 controls of European ancestry from 11 cohorts showed an association of the A allele with SLE (allelic OR 1.32, p = 1.04 x 10(-9)).

subject: CSK rs34933034 (G > A)
object: CSK

subject: Manjarrez-Orduño et al. (2012)
object: Manjarrez-Orduño et al. (2012) showed that the rs34933034 A allele lies almost exclusively on the CSK B haplotype (D-prime = 0.95) but has low correlation (r2 < 0.5) with other haplotype-tagging SNPs; conditional analysis with 1000 Genomes imputation showed that association of B-haplotype tags such as rs8033381 (P = 9 x 10(-8)) was eliminated after conditioning on rs34933034 (P = 0.19). No genetic interaction was observed between rs34933034 and PTPN22 R620W (rs2476601).

subject: Manjarrez-Orduño et al. (2012)
object: Manjarrez-Orduño et al. (2012) found that CSK expression was highest in B cells and inversely correlated with B-cell maturity, and in naive B cells from 29 healthy B-haplotype homozygous donors the rs34933034 risk A allele was associated with higher CSK transcript levels. Naive B cells from risk allele carriers showed increased inhibitory Tyr508 phosphorylation of Lyn, enhanced calcium mobilization after BCR cross-linking, and carriers had higher plasma IgM.

subject: Manjarrez-Orduño et al. (2012)
object: Manjarrez-Orduño et al. (2012) found in 27 umbilical cord blood samples that newborns homozygous for the CSK risk allele had double the frequency of transitional B cells, with an expansion of late transitional cells; the authors suggested this might reflect impaired tolerance checkpoint or enhanced positive selection, predicting more autoreactive B cells, and that the Lyp-Csk complex increases lupus susceptibility at multiple B-cell maturation and activation points.

subject: Mueller et al. (2013)
object: Mueller et al. (2013) mapped allelic and paralogous sequence variation across the FCGR2/FCGR3 locus on chromosome 1q23 using sequence from fosmid and BAC clones and sequence-captured DNA from FCGR3B-deleted genomes. They identified two highly paralogous 24.5-kb blocks within the FCGR2C/FCGR3B/FCGR2B locus, devoid of nonpolymorphic paralogous sequence variations, that define the limits of the regions in which nonallelic homologous recombination leads to FCGR2C/FCGR3B copy-number variation; reduced FCGR3B copy number is associated with increased SLE risk.

subject: FCGR3B FCGR3B deletion
object: FCGR3B

subject: Mueller et al. (2013)
object: Mueller et al. (2013) found by flow cytometry, immunoblotting, and cDNA sequencing that individuals with FCGR3B-deleted alleles showed ectopic presence of FcγRIIb on natural killer (NK) cells. They concluded that FCGR3B deletion juxtaposes the 5-prime regulatory sequences of FCGR2C with the coding sequence of FCGR2B, creating a chimeric gene that results in ectopic FcγRIIb accumulation on NK cells, providing an explanation for SLE risk associated with reduced FCGR3B copy number.

subject: Mueller et al. (2013)
object: Mueller et al. (2013) found evidence of swapping of haplotype blocks between the highly paralogous blocks of the FCGR2/FCGR3 locus, most likely arising from sequential ancestral recombination events across the region.

subject: Kshirsagar et al. (2014)
object: Kshirsagar et al. (2014) found that effector T cells (CD4+CD45RA-Foxp3- and Foxp3-low) from children with lupus nephritis had enhanced Stat3 activity, which correlated with increased frequencies of IL-17-producing cells. PBMCs from these children had significantly higher RORC and IL-17 mRNA levels than controls. Inhibiting mTOR with rapamycin reduced both Stat3 activation and the frequency of IL-17-producing T cells.

subject: Kshirsagar et al. (2014)
object: Kshirsagar et al. (2014) showed that Th17 cells from children with lupus nephritis had high Akt activity and an enhanced capacity to migrate, and that inhibiting the Akt pathway significantly reduced Th17 cell migration. Complement factor C5a slightly increased IL-17 expression and activated Akt in anti-CD3-activated lupus effector T cells. The authors suggested that modulating Akt activity therapeutically might inhibit Th17 cell trafficking to sites of inflammation.

subject: Talaei et al. (2015)
object: Talaei et al. (2015) studied C57BL/6 congenic mice carrying a homozygous NZB chromosome 1 interval from 70 to 100 cM. These mice develop high-titer antinuclear antibodies and severe glomerulonephritis. Using subcongenic mice, the authors found that a locus in the 88-96 cM region was associated with altered dendritic cell (DC) function. This locus synergized with T-cell defects to promote expansion of pathogenic proinflammatory T-cell subsets.

subject: Talaei et al. (2015)
object: Talaei et al. (2015) found that the promoter region of the NZB gene encoding EWS-activated transcript 2 (EAT-2), an adapter in the SLAM signaling pathway, is polymorphic. This polymorphism reduced EAT-2 levels in dendritic cells by about 70%. Silencing EAT-2 in DCs lacking the polymorphism increased IL-12 production and enhanced Th1 differentiation in T cell-DC cocultures. This reproduced the phenotype of DCs from congenic mice carrying the NZB chromosome 1 70-100 cM interval.

subject: EAT-2 NZB EAT-2 promoter polymorphism
object: EAT-2

subject: Talaei et al. (2015)
object: Talaei et al. (2015) showed that SLAM signaling inhibited IL-12 production by CD40L-activated dendritic cells, and that EAT-2 knockdown increased IL-12 production by CD40-stimulated DCs. SLAM coengagement blocked CD40-induced activation of the p38 MAPK and JNK pathways. This block was reversed in DCs carrying the NZB EAT-2 allele. The authors concluded that EAT-2 negatively regulates DC cytokine production downstream of SLAM engagement and that a polymorphism disturbing this process promotes the development of lupus.

subject: Zhao et al. (2017)
object: Zhao et al. (2017) genotyped SLE cases and controls of Chinese, European American, and African American ancestry with the Immunochip. In Chinese, the strongest association was at rs73366469 in the GTF2IRD1-GTF2I intergenic region on 7q11.23 (P = 3.8 x 10(-29), OR = 2.88). The association was confirmed at a modest level in European Americans but not in African Americans. A non-Immunochip SNP, rs117026326 in intron 9 of GTF2I, showed stronger association and accounted for the rs73366469 signal.

subject: Zhao et al. (2017)
object: Zhao et al. (2017) used NCF1-specific PCR and Sanger sequencing to resequence the 15.5-kb NCF1 region in 45 Chinese subjects, which was needed to distinguish NCF1 from its pseudogenes NCF1B and NCF1C. They identified a missense variant in NCF1 (g.74779296G>A; p.Arg90His, rs201802880) as the likely causal variant behind the 7q11.23 SLE association. The risk allele was associated with SLE in African Americans (15.7% vs 8.3%, OR = 2.02), in Asians (meta-analysis of Chinese and Korean datasets, P = 3.1 x 10(-104), OR = 3.47), and in European Americans (meta P = 1.9 x 10(-7), OR = 2.61). Conditioning on p.Arg90His eliminated the signals at p.Ser99Gly and in the GTF2IRD1-GTF2I region.

subject: NCF1 g.74779296G>A / p.R90H
object: NCF1

subject: Zhao et al. (2017)
object: Zhao et al. (2017) found that the NCF1 p.Arg90His risk allele was associated with earlier age of SLE onset in a dose-dependent manner in Korean and European American patients.

subject: Zhao et al. (2017)
object: Zhao et al. (2017) found that NCF1 p.Arg90His was also associated with primary Sjogren syndrome in Chinese (OR = 2.45) and European Americans (OR = 2.35). It was also associated with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis in Koreans (OR = 1.65), with a modest effect size.

subject: Zhao et al. (2017)
object: Zhao et al. (2017) assessed NCF1 copy number variation using the deltaGT/GTGT ratio. Having one copy of NCF1 was associated with increased SLE risk in Koreans, Chinese, and European Americans (P = 5.9 x 10(-4), OR = 3.91). Having 3 or more copies was protective in Koreans, Chinese, European Americans, and African Americans. The authors concluded that this supports reduced ROS production as a risk factor for SLE.

subject: Zhao et al. (2017)
object: Zhao et al. (2017) noted that Arg90 of p47phox lies in a phosphoinositide-binding pocket of the PX domain and is critical for p47phox membrane translocation and NOX2 activation. Prior in vitro mutation studies indicated that the Arg90His change reduces ROS production. The authors suggested that p.Arg90His confers SLE risk by reducing NOX2-derived ROS levels. However, the genotype was not associated with intracellular ROS levels in neutrophils from controls, and rs117026326 genotype was not associated with NCF1 transcript levels.

subject: Bialas et al. (2017)
object: Bialas et al. (2017) reported behavioral phenotypes and synapse loss in lupus-prone mice. Blocking type I interferon (IFN) signaling prevented both. Type I IFN stimulated microglia to become reactive and to engulf neuronal and synaptic material in these mice.

subject: Bialas et al. (2017)
object: Bialas et al. (2017) observed increased type I IFN signaling in postmortem hippocampal brain sections from patients with SLE. They suggested that IFN-driven, microglia-dependent synapse loss may explain the neurologic symptoms seen in some patients with SLE (CNS lupus).

subject: Bialas et al. (2017)
object: Bialas et al. (2017) noted that up to 75% of patients with SLE have neuropsychiatric symptoms, collectively called CNS lupus. These range from anxiety, depression and cognitive impairment to seizures and, rarely, psychosis. CNS lupus typically presents at diagnosis or within the first year.

subject: Farias et al. (2019)
object: Farias et al. (2019) performed targeted resequencing of coding and conserved regulatory regions in and around 215 candidate genes in pooled DNA from 140 SLE patients and 17 Swedish controls. They identified a rare variant, rs200395694:G>T (hg19 chr1:g.156450591G>T), in intron 4 of the MEF2D gene that was associated with SLE in Swedish cohorts. The combined cohorts had 12 heterozygotes among 504 patients and 6 among 839 controls (allele frequency 0.011 vs 0.003; p = 0.014). The allele frequency was 0.001 in 1000 Genomes and 0.002 in SweFreq, and no homozygotes were reported.

subject: MEF2D rs200395694:G > T (hg19 chr1:g.156450591 G > T)
object: MEF2D

subject: Farias et al. (2019)
object: Among 140 Swedish SLE patients with clinical data, Farias et al. (2019) found that all 3 carriers of the MEF2D rs200395694 risk allele (2 females, 1 male) had anti-Sm antibodies, anti-RNP antibodies, and Raynaud phenomenon. This triad was present in 8.7% of all patients, and its association with the variant was significant (p = 0.00037). Associations with anti-Sm alone (p = 0.0058) and anti-RNP alone (p = 0.017) were nominally significant.

subject: MEF2D rs200395694-A
object: MEF2D

subject: Farias et al. (2019)
object: Farias et al. (2019) found that the MEF2D rs200395694 region carries marks of a cell type-specific enhancer that is active in T, B, NK cells, and monocytes. In EMSA, the alleles differed in protein binding in Jurkat and Daudi nuclear extracts. In luciferase assays, the alternative A allele increased expression in unstimulated Jurkat (1.3-fold) and K562 (1.8-fold) cells but suppressed expression in THP-1 cells. In minigene assays, the risk allele significantly repressed splicing of the alternative tissue-specific alpha-2 isoform in all cell lines tested without affecting the alpha-1 isoform. The authors suggested that this could change the set of target genes regulated by alpha-2, which includes DNASE1L3 and AIM2.

subject: MEF2D rs200395694
object: MEF2D

subject: Kamitaki et al. (2020)
object: Kamitaki et al. (2020) built a multi-ancestry reference panel of 2,530 haplotypes from whole-genome sequencing of 1,265 individuals. They used it to impute C4A and C4B gene copy number into ImmunoChip data from 6,748 SLE cases and 11,516 controls of European ancestry. Across the 11 most common combinations of C4A and C4B copy number, relative risk of SLE varied 7-fold. Each copy of C4A was protective (OR 0.54), equivalent to 2.3 copies of C4B (OR 0.77).

subject: Kamitaki et al. (2020)
object: Kamitaki et al. (2020) analyzed SLE risk for individual C4 alleles and their flanking SNP haplotypes. They concluded that C4A gives strong protection and C4B more modest protection against SLE, and that the C4 genes themselves, rather than nearby variants, are the main drivers of risk. The C4-B(S) allele, which lacks any C4A gene, was the highest-risk C4 allele.

subject: Kamitaki et al. (2020)
object: Kamitaki et al. (2020) studied an African American cohort of 1,494 SLE cases and 5,908 controls, in which LD between C4-B(S) and HLA-DRB1*03:01 is low (r2 = 0.10). A joint association analysis implicated C4A (p < 10(-14)) and C4B (p < 10(-5)) but not DRB1*03:01 (p = 0.29). C4-B(S) alleles increased SLE risk regardless of DRB1*03:01 status. Each C4 allele had a similar effect size in Europeans and African Americans.

subject: Kamitaki et al. (2020)
object: Kamitaki et al. (2020) jointly analyzed the European and African American SLE cohorts while accounting for C4 alleles. This identified a more modest genetic effect independent of C4, tagged by rs2105898 and rs9271513. It appeared to involve noncoding variation in the HLA class II XL9 region that is associated with expression levels of many HLA class II genes.

subject: Kamitaki et al. (2020)
object: Kamitaki et al. (2020) found that C4 alleles had stronger effects on SLE risk in men than in women. A sex-by-C4 interaction term was significant (p = 0.002). Common combinations of C4A and C4B produced 14-fold variation in SLE risk among men versus 6-fold among women.

subject: Kamitaki et al. (2020)
object: Kamitaki et al. (2020) measured complement in CSF from 589 adults. Per C4 gene copy, men had on average 27% more C4 protein than women, and C3 levels were 42% higher in men. Plasma data showed the sex difference was most pronounced at ages 20 to 50 years, which matches the ages of differential disease vulnerability. The authors suggested that sex differences in complement levels may help explain why women have a greater risk of SLE.

subject: Kamitaki et al. (2020)
object: Kamitaki et al. (2020) proposed that higher C4 protein levels may attenuate interactions between the adaptive immune system and ribonuclear self-antigens at sites of cell injury, because complement speeds clearance of debris from dead cells, and that this could pre-empt the development of autoimmunity. They noted that the same C4 alleles that increase vulnerability to schizophrenia appeared to protect strongly against SLE.
